The Palestinian Authority backs a two-state solution but Palestinian armed group Hamas does not because it is opposed to the existence of Israel.
Hamas says that it could accept an interim Palestinian state based on 1967 de facto borders, without officially recognising Israel, if refugees were given the right to return.
Israel has built about 160 settlements housing 700,000 Jews since it occupied the West Bank and East Jerusalem during the 1967 Middle East war. An estimated 3.3 million Palestinians live alongside them.
There has been a surge in attacks by settlers on Palestinians and their property in the West Bank since the start of the Gaza war, which was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on Israel on 7 October 2023.
  - Published29 July
 ![Screengrabs from a video showing a teenage Israeli settler using a stick to hit a metal gate and fence during an attack on a Palestinian home in the village of al-Mughayyir, near Ramallah, in the Israeli-occupied West Bank (11 July 2026)](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/1a9c/live/a9fea910-8aa2-11f1-a7ab-8b30adf0800a.jpg)
  - Published21 hours ago
 ![Palestinian kids walk to school. They are wearing blue school uniforms.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/1ded/live/26dbafb0-aaff-11f1-a2a8-b5ca0233056a.jpg)
summary: The UK has announced a comprehensive sanctions regime targeting illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, accusing the Israeli government of turning a blind eye to the ethnic cleansing of Palestinians. In response, Israel's Foreign Minister Gideon Saar denounced the move as an outrageous lie and announced counter-measures, including shutting down the UK's consulate in East Jerusalem and banning several British MPs from entering the country. The UK's actions, launched alongside France and Canada, are intended to protect the viability of the two-state solution amid growing international condemnation of settlement expansion.
key_points: The UK announced sanctions on illegal West Bank settlements, banning settlement goods and targeting companies and individuals supporting settlement expansion.
Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband accused Israel of turning a blind eye to settler-perpetrated ethnic cleansing against Palestinians.
Israel's Foreign Minister Gideon Saar condemned the measures as hostile and announced the closure of the UK's consulate in East Jerusalem alongside entry bans for 11 UK MPs.
France and Canada joined the UK in a joint statement emphasizing their commitment to protecting the two-state solution.

title: Saudi-Houthi fighting in Yemen escalates: What happened, and what’s next?
author: Usaid Siddiqui
content:
![This screen grab taken from video footage released on September 8, 2026 by the Saudi-backed National Resistance Forces in Yemen shows a fighter firing a rocket-propelled grenade (RPG), as Yemeni government forces and National Resistance Forces fire at Houthi fighters on the Kadha front, west of the city of Taiz in Yemen's western Taiz province. Yemen's Houthi rebels struck a series of targets in Saudi Arabia on September 8, wounding 73, in their heaviest attack since the conflict reignited during the Middle East war. (Photo by Yemen National Resistance Forces / AFP) / RESTRICTED TO EDITORIAL USE - MANDATORY CREDIT "AFP PHOTO / NATIONAL RESISTANCE FORCES IN YEMEN / HANDOUT" - NO MARKETING NO ADVERTISING CAMPAIGNS - DISTRIBUTED AS A SERVICE TO CLIENTS](https://www.aljazeera.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/AFP__20260908__C7M72CV__v2__HighRes__TopshotYemenSaudiHouthiConflict-1788857659.jpg?resize=770%2C513&quality=80)
Yemen’s Houthi group has carried out attacks in southern Saudi Arabia, with Riyadh saying that dozens of people have been wounded, as fighting between the Iran-aligned group and pro-Saudi forces in Yemen sharply escalates.
The Houthis on Tuesday said they targeted Saudi energy sites belonging to oil giant Saudi Aramco in southern areas, with the group’s military spokesperson calling it “a broad operation”.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3‘Breaks my heart’: Yemen jab shortages spark fears for millions of children
- list 2 of 3How significant are the Yemeni government’s military gains against Houthis?
- list 3 of 3Yemen gov’t forces launch air strikes on Houthi targets
Saudi authorities confirmed attacks on several facilities and installations related to the energy sector in the south of the country, vowing a firm response. Riyadh also accused the Houthis of wounding at least 73 people in the attacks.
The conflict between the Yemeni armed group and Saudi Arabia is unfolding as the Houthis are currently fighting Yemen’s Riyadh-backed internationally recognised government, which announced that it was launching counteroffensives against Houthi-held positions across several provinces on Monday.
The renewed hostilities are the most serious since a United Nations-brokered truce halted large-scale fighting in 2022, after eight years of a full-blown conflict that killed tens of thousands of people in one of the world’s poorest countries.
The escalation also comes as the strategic importance of Yemen’s Bab al-Mandeb Strait grows amid Iran’s effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz, a key passageway for global oil and gas supplies.
The Houthis have sought to advance towards the vital Red Sea shipping route, while government forces say their campaign ultimately aims to retake the Houthi-held capital, Sanaa.
So what do we know about the latest fighting, and what comes next?
How did the fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis unfold?
The Houthis on Monday said Saudi Arabia launched multiple attacks on Houthi-held areas.
The group said Saudi attacks using aircraft and cruise missiles struck al-Jawf, al-Bayda, Marib and Taiz provinces.
Moreover, the Houthis accused Saudi Arabia of carrying out an air strike on a prison in al-Hazm, the capital of al-Jawf, killing seven people and injuring seven others. Riyadh did not immediately comment on the attacks.
At the same time, the Houthis claimed to have shot down Saudi reconnaissance drones over al-Jawf and al-Bayda.
Meanwhile, on Tuesday, Major-General Turki al-Malki, the Saudi spokesman for the Riyadh-led coalition in Yemen, said the Houthis carried out attacks on the Saudi cities of Abha, Khamis Mushait, Jizan and Najran, injuring at least 73 people, among them women and children.
According to a statement from Saudi Arabia’s Energy Ministry, the strikes also triggered fires at multiple oil installations and utility sites across the kingdom’s southern provinces.
Southern Saudi Arabia is home to key oil infrastructure, including the Jizan refinery, one of the kingdom’s largest, with the capacity to process 400,000 barrels of crude per day.
Shortly after, the Houthis announced that they had targeted Saudi energy infrastructure operated by oil giant Aramco in the south using drones and ballistic missiles.
The group’s military spokesman, Yahya Saree, said the attacks were retaliation for recent Saudi attacks on Houthi-controlled areas across Yemen. Later on Tuesday, Houthi-affiliated media Al Maisrah said Saudi forces had targeted the Al-Jubah district in Marib in the Houthi-controlled part of Yemen.
Saudi Arabia’s Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan al Saud said the kingdom “strongly condemns” the Houthis’ attacks.
“The Houthis choose to prioritise their narrow interests over the interests of Yemen and resort to violence,” Prince Faisal said in a joint press conference with Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov in Moscow.
However, Prince Faisal said diplomacy is still possible with the Houthis to end the fighting after heavy strikes on the country.
“The road to diplomacy is not closed,” he said. “Saudi Arabia will always support diplomatic solutions, but the kingdom will never hesitate to defend itself and its interests. We will use every tool to do our job and our duties.”
Why is this escalation taking place now?
A key focus of the fighting is the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, the narrow waterway connecting the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden.
The Houthis declared a blockade against Saudi shipping in July. The Houthis have also pushed towards government-held areas near al-Makha (Mocha) and territory bordering the Bab al-Mandeb Strait amid reinforcements and counteroffensives from government forces.
The strait’s strategic importance has increased dramatically because Iran’s restrictions on the Strait of Hormuz have forced Saudi Arabia to rely more heavily on its Red Sea export route. Between March and mid-July, Saudi seaborne crude exports through Bab al-Mandeb were eight times higher than during the same period in 2025.
In 2024, about 4.1 million barrels of crude oil and petroleum products passed through the strait daily on average – about 5 percent of the global total.
![Internally displaced (IDP) Yemeni women who fled their homes with their families due to renewed clashes between Yemen's Saudi-backed government forces and the country's Houthi rebels, carry jerrycans after seeking shelter in Mocha, on the Red Sea coast of Yemen on September 7, 2026. \[AFP\]](https://www.aljazeera.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/afp_6a9f3c52918a-1788820562.jpg?w=770&resize=770%2C513&quality=80)
Ahmed Nagi, a senior analyst at the International Crisis Group, said the strait holds importance “when we look at the Houthis’ broader strategy”.
“The move towards the western coast is not only about gaining territory on the ground. It also has a maritime dimension,” he told Al Jazeera.
“The Houthis have already linked their military campaign to the Red Sea and the shipping routes around Bab al-Mandeb. So gaining more control over the … western coast could give them greater depth and allow them to sustain pressure on maritime traffic in the Red Sea. In that sense, the ground offensive and their maritime campaign are closely connected.”
The latest escalation also follows fighting that resumed in July after an Iranian aircraft attempted to land in Sanaa without Saudi authorisation, followed by strikes on Sanaa airport and Houthi retaliation.
What has been the international reaction?
- Qatar: The Foreign Ministry said the attacks represent a “reprehensible act of aggression and an unacceptable disregard for the lives of civilians”.
- Bahrain: The latest attacks “represent a dangerous escalation [and] a flagrant violation of the rules of international law”, the country’s Foreign Ministry said.
- United Arab Emirates: Abu Dhabi, in addition to condemning the attacks, also decried the continued targeting of commercial vessels in the Red Sea.
- Russia: Foreign Minister Lavrov said Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia were “counterproductive” and were damaging the global economy.
- Pakistan: Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif called the attack “cowardly”, adding that such “treacherous attacks threaten the lives of innocent people as well as regional peace and security”.
What is happening between government forces and the Houthis?
On Sunday, Yemen’s internationally recognised government said its warplanes had struck Houthi positions in Hodeidah, Marib and al-Jawf, as fighting spread across several fronts.
On Monday, government-aligned forces stepped up their counteroffensive. They announced a ground push towards the al-Labanat mountains in al-Jawf, while also reporting rocket attacks on Yatma and “intensive battles” with Houthi fighters in the province. Government forces also claimed advances towards Dhi Na’im district in al-Bayda.
The Houthis said they had repelled the advance towards al-Labanat and inflicted casualties on government-aligned forces. Houthi official Mohammed al-Farah also claimed the group fired ballistic missiles at reinforcements in al-Jawf.
By late Monday, government-aligned forces reported carrying out further air attacks against Houthi positions west of Taiz.
Al Jazeera could not independently verify the battlefield claims by the Houthis or the Yemeni government.
Rashad al-Alimi, who heads Yemen’s Saudi-backed Presidential Leadership Council, meanwhile said on Monday that government forces had made significant gains against the Houthis, pointing to advances in al-Jawf, al-Bayda, Taiz and Hodeidah.
“Our armed forces will continue to carry out their constitutional duty until state institutions are restored and their authority extends over the entire territory of Yemen,” al-Alimi said in a statement.
Yemen’s deputy defence minister, Major-General Samir al-Sabri, said in comments aired on state television that the government had resolved to “retake Sanaa”.
Majid al-Nuzaili, a spokesperson for government-aligned forces, said the goal of the offensive was to “liberate Yemen from the grip” of the Houthis “and restore Sanaa as a capital for all Yemenis”.
What is the humanitarian situation on the ground?
The World Health Organization said on Monday that at least 728 people have been killed or wounded in Yemen since August 23, with the majority in Taiz and along the western coast.
It said an estimated 21,000 people, roughly 3,000 families, have been displaced from Taiz alone since Thursday.
“Families are arriving with nothing: no shelter, no food, no way to know if it’s safe to go back,” said Abdusattor Esoev, head of the International Organization for Migration’s mission in Yemen. “Many of these are people who have already been displaced once, twice, even four times before.”
Al Jazeera’s Yousef Mawry, reporting from Sanaa, said the casualty count is expected to rise.
“These casualties are said to be in the hundreds from both sides, especially as we have reports of air strikes being conducted in the governorate of al-Jawf,” he said.
The Crisis Group’s Nagi said the world was witnessing “significant deterioration in what is already a catastrophic situation”.
“We saw in the past few days a lot of displacement from areas where there has been fighting between the two sides, especially in Taiz,” he noted.
“Those are the direct impacts, but there are also indirect ones. The economic situation is likely to get worse, which will put even more pressure on the humanitarian situation. Ultimately, I think it will depend on how long this round of fighting lasts. The longer the conflict continues, the greater the humanitarian impact will be.”
What’s next?
Analyst Hisham al-Omeisy said the fighting in the war-torn country was no longer simply a domestic issue.
“We are way beyond the concept [of it] being domestic. It all started with the Houthis pushing to control Bab al-Mandeb and the western coast, to control the chokehold on the other side of the Arabian Peninsula, with the Iranians controlling the Strait of Hormuz,” al-Omeisy, a senior Yemen adviser at the European Institute of Peace, told Al Jazeera.
“This is definitely not domestic, especially when the Houthis have started attacking Saudi Arabia as well for the better part of the last month, and now escalating since today [Tuesday].”
Domestically, the Crisis Group’s Nagi said it was “unclear” what the outcome of this round of fighting will be, describing the situation on the ground as “very fluid”.
“But what we are seeing is that the government seems to be in a stronger position than at any time before, and it sees this round of fighting as an opportunity to consolidate its position and gain more territory from the Houthis,” he said, while warning that this did not mean the Houthis were weak.
“It’s true that the Houthis are fighting in Taiz, and they were the ones who launched the offensive against government forces there and made some gains. But on other fronts, in al-Jawf, al-Bayda, Marib and elsewhere, government forces have advanced and gained several key areas, while the Houthis have been on the defensive.”
On whether there will be a winner in this conflict, al-Omeisy said that in the long term, he expects a negotiated settlement.
“Look at the history of Yemen … we always inevitably reach some sort of a deal, so it’s not going to be a winner-takes-all,” he said.
“I don’t imagine there’s going to be a push to regain the capital [Sanaa], for instance. It’s going to be a bloodbath if they [government-aligned forces] do that.”
“There’s going to be a humbling of the Houthi forces. There’s going to be losses. But eventually, you will need a political deal,” al-Omeisy added.
According to Saudi political analyst Khaled Batarfi, the Houthi strikes will trigger a response, but not a prolonged war.
“This is an escalation, of course,” Batarfi told Al Jazeera. In past attacks, Saudi Arabia tried “to not get engaged in a civil war, keep its distance, and to not respond to attacks. But now this is too much [of an escalation],” he said.
“The coalition will have a say on that,” Batarfi noted. “This is a civil war inside Yemen, and it affects us as one of the parties. And so any response … in the same way [will be] an eye for an eye. But I don’t see a prolonged war – not with Iran, and not with the Houthis.”
summary: Fighting between Yemen's Houthi rebels and pro-Saudi forces has sharply escalated, culminating in Houthi drone and missile strikes that wounded 73 people and damaged energy infrastructure in southern Saudi Arabia. The renewed conflict is the most serious since a 2022 truce and coincides with a strategic push by the Houthis toward the Bab al-Mandeb Strait. While Saudi Arabia has vowed to defend itself and condemned the attacks, the kingdom's foreign minister stated that the path to diplomacy remains open.
key_points: Houthi strikes on southern Saudi Arabia targeted energy sites belonging to Saudi Aramco and wounded at least 73 people.
The escalation follows counteroffensives launched by Yemen's Riyadh-backed government across multiple provinces.
The strategic importance of the Bab al-Mandeb Strait has amplified the conflict as the Houthis push toward the vital Red Sea shipping route.
The renewed fighting has displaced thousands of civilians and severely worsened the humanitarian situation in Yemen.

title: Eiffel Tower reopens after protest over removing women staff
author: AFP; Reuters
content:
![Hindu monks take part in a religious ceremony in front of the Eiffel Tower.](https://www.aljazeera.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/AFP__20260903__C79B3WE__v1__HighRes__FranceReligionHinduismBaps-1788848635.jpg?resize=770%2C513&quality=80)
The Eiffel Tower has reopened after staff walked out over the removal of women staff during a weekend visit by a Hindu religious delegation.
The operating company that runs the Paris landmark, SETE, acknowledged that the group had requested the Saturday visit be organised to limit “interactions with women” and said “these conditions should not have been accepted.”
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Protests as India’s Hindu nationalists take centre stage in New York
- list 2 of 3RSS chief’s visit to US denounced as ‘goodwill tour’ for Hindu nationalism
- list 3 of 3Oneness or Hindu supremacy? RSS chief Bhagwat’s secretive New York hosts
It said the landmark would reopen on Tuesday following a meeting the previous day between staff and management over the incident, which has also drawn criticism from French politicians.
On its website, the Eiffel Tower said the iconic monument was “open today”. Shortly before 9:30am (7:30 GMT), visitors were passing through security checkpoints at the foot of the tower, a journalist with the AFP news agency said.
The Bochasanwasi Akshar Purushottam Swaminarayan Sanstha (BAPS) spiritual movement apologised for “any pain or inconvenience caused” by their visit.
“To the best of our knowledge, at no point was anyone prevented access to the Eiffel Tower,” the organisation wrote on social media.
“Due to the size of our delegation, the visit was arranged in conjunction with the Eiffel Tower team at the start of normal operating hours to avoid disrupting or inconveniencing others.”
Eiffel Tower staff said in a statement that they condemned “professional instructions that led to female employees being sidelined, replaced and made invisible because of their sex” during the visit by the delegation.
“Some were asked to leave their posts and withdraw to other areas. In some posts they were replaced by men. And all female employees were instructed not to go through or cross certain areas while the delegation was present,” staff said, adding they were shocked to have been put in such a situation.
Paris Mayor Emmanuel Gregoire said an investigation would be launched “as soon as possible”. In a post on social media, he said he was aware of the employees’ anger and agreed their dissatisfaction was legitimate.
Yael Braun-Pivet, president of the National Assembly, wrote in a post on social media: “Welcoming others never means giving up our values. In France, women are fully present in public life. No one tells them to become invisible.”
summary: The Eiffel Tower has reopened following a staff walkout prompted by the removal of female employees during a weekend visit by a Hindu religious delegation. The operating company, SETE, admitted that the delegation's request to limit interactions with women should not have been accepted. Staff condemned the directives that sidelined women, and French officials announced that an investigation would be launched into the incident.
key_points: The Eiffel Tower reopened on Tuesday after a meeting between staff and management.
Staff walked out because female employees were sidelined and replaced by men during a visit by a Hindu religious delegation.
The operating company SETE acknowledged that the delegation's request to limit interactions with women should not have been accepted.
The BAPS spiritual movement apologized for any pain or inconvenience caused by their visit.
Paris Mayor Emmanuel Gregoire stated that an investigation would be launched as soon as possible.

title: Ratko Mladić, the ‘Butcher of Bosnia’, given hero’s funeral in Serbia
author: Oliver Holmes
content:
Ratko Mladić, a Serbian general convicted of orchestrating the worst massacre in Europe since the second world war, has been given a hero’s funeral attended by thousands in Belgrade despite international alarm.
Known as the “Butcher of Bosnia” for his role during the Balkans genocide in the 1990s, Mladić died in prison in late August aged 84 while serving a life sentence for war crimes and crimes against humanity.
Mladić was found guilty of genocide in 2017 for his role in the 1995 Srebrenica massacre, in which about 8,000 Bosniak Muslim men and boys were killed after Bosnian Serb forces overran the UN-designated enclave.
But he has remained a beloved figure among many Serbs, with the president, Aleksandar Vučić, arguing last month for him to be released early from a UN detention facility in The Hague so he could die on Serbian soil.
Vučić, an ultranationalist leader, has dominated Serbian politics for more than a decade and is due to run again for prime minister in a snap election announced on Monday.
Mladić’s coffin was flown to Serbia last week on a government plane, draped in national flags and carried from the aircraft by uniformed soldiers.
On Monday morning, thousands of people gathered in front of a small church in the Serbian capital to pay their respects to Mladić. Armed forces stood guard at his casket, on top of which was laid his signature military cap, as well as a sword. A display of medals lay in front.
“We know that his name will remain deeply etched in the memory and prayers of the majority of our Serbian Orthodox people, who feel and nurture a deep sense of gratitude towards him,” said Porfirije, the patriarch of the Serbian Orthodox church.
After the service, a street procession moved with the coffin towards the cemetery, where Mladić was buried with military honours including a three-volley rifle firing salute.
![crowd and mourners including Serbian veteran soldiers queuing](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/ceb11ed4db8558b31672ba9b858176d11adb483d/0_0_3587_2391/master/3587.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Scenes of military pomp drew condemnation from the European Union’s enlargement commissioner, Marta Kos, who cancelled a forthcoming visit to Serbia on Friday. “The return of his remains to Belgrade reminds Europe of the darkest pages in our recent history,” she said on social media.
![A crowd of people watch the funeral service on a large screen in front of a white stone Serbian Orthodox church with blue domes.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/984a2b0fb7dbc9d1f722d9993f7c13f37c4b6779/0_0_7000_4667/master/7000.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Serbia has been negotiating EU accession since 2014, but the process has stalled in recent years.
“The glorification surrounding [Mladić’s] death is incompatible with the values on which the EU path is built,” said Kos. “That path requires confronting the past, genuine reconciliation and respecting the victims of war crimes.”
![Men wearing Serbian flags as capes, each with a large picture of Ratko Mladić on them which appears across their backs, stand among people gathered outside a pale stone church which has a gold-decorated icon over the doorway.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/ae934ad183b569a01c7ab241111a558b095bb1f9/0_0_6000_4000/master/6000.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
An EU spokesperson repeated the warning on Monday. “Any glorification of war criminals, genocide denial and revisionism contradict the most fundamental European values and have no place in the EU or in EU candidate countries,” he said in a statement.
On Sunday evening, football fans displayed a huge image of Mladić and chanted his name at a match in Belgrade.
While Monday’s ceremony was not an official state funeral – probably to avoid further damaging international relations – it mirrored a state event, with large police and military delegations. Vučić said he had a prior engagement, but his son Danilo attended along with several other Serbian ministers, as well as Russia’s ambassador to the country.
During the early 1990s Balkans conflict, when Mladić was a military officer, Vučić was entering politics as part of the Serbian Radical party, a far-right nationalist party that sought to secure land for a “Greater Serbia” by removing non-Serb populations.
Decades later, Vučić has managed to remain in office – once as prime minister and twice as president over 12 years – while vacillating between keeping close ties with Russia and seeking EU membership. But anti-government anger was galvanised after the 2024 collapse of a railway station roof that killed 16 people, with widespread claims of corruption threatening his hold on power.
On Monday, Serbia’s government said it intends to dissolve parliament and set a date for a snap election, a year ahead of a planned December 2027 vote. The current prime minister, Djuro Macut, said: “If we want to mitigate tensions in society there is no better way than to ask people.”
after newsletter promotion
The election has been seen as a chance for Vučić, who cannot legally run for president for a third term, to stay in high office, and his ruling party has nominated him for prime minister.
Marko Vujić, an assistant professor at the Faculty of Political Sciences at the University of Belgrade, said he did not believe the government had planned the snap election announcement to coincide with Mladić’s funeral. “But once his death occurred, the regime took advantage of the momentum surrounding the event and used that day, among other things, for the dissolution of parliament.”
![Serbian military service personnel pay their respects at Mladić’s coffin](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/f2391a1c4ea62e491e3b16861562a56862fc8cd2/0_0_7000_4667/master/7000.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Mladić was one of the main architects of the policy of ethnic cleansing during the Bosnian war, which killed more than 100,000 people and displaced more than 2 million.
Key among his crimes was the 1,460-day siege of the Bosnian capital, Sarajevo, where the civilian population was subjected to daily shelling and sniper attacks from Serb nationalist forces, and more than 10,000 people were killed.
The three-year conflict culminated in the 1995 killing of at least 8,000 Bosniak Muslims in the town of Srebrenica, a crime that shocked governments in Europe that had spent decades working to prevent mass killings after the mid-century horrors when Nazi Germany killed 6 million Jews.
![Gen Ratko Mladić in Sarajevo, April 1993.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/59aa9e83a2077178fc71c2ccf114ddec9126cbc0/0_0_3228_2546/master/3228.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
In Srebrenica, Mladić’s forces were filmed handing out sweets to children and promising their safe passage before thousands of Bosnian men and boys were rounded up, killed, and their bodies bulldozed into mass graves. “We give this town to the Serb people as a gift,” Mladić said at the time in filmed comments.
The killings have been pointed to as an international failure, especially as Srebrenica had been designated a “safe haven” under the protection of the UN, a global body created immediately after the second world war specifically to help prevent such bloody future global conflicts.
Mladić was arrested in Serbia in 2011 after 16 years as a fugitive, and sentenced by a UN tribunal in the Netherlands to life imprisonment in 2017.
While in detention, Mladić had been in ill health after having a series of strokes.
The Balkan war started after the June 1991 breakup of Yugoslavia, when Slovenia and Croatia declared independence. Bosnian Serbs quickly took control of more than two-thirds of Bosnia and launched the siege of Sarajevo. After three years of bloodshed, the Dayton agreement was signed in Dayton, Ohio, ending the war and creating the independent state of Bosnia and Herzegovina.
- 
  Agence France-Presse contributed to this report
summary: Ratko Mladić, the convicted war criminal known as the "Butcher of Bosnia," received a hero's funeral in Belgrade attended by thousands of mourners, soldiers, and officials. Mladić died in prison in late August while serving a life sentence for genocide and crimes against humanity, including the 1995 Srebrenica massacre and the siege of Sarajevo. The military-style funeral drew sharp international condemnation from the European Union, which warned that the glorification of war criminals contradicts EU values and stalled accession paths.
key_points: Ratko Mladić was convicted of genocide in 2017 for his role in the 1995 Srebrenica massacre and died in prison in late August while serving a life sentence.
Thousands of people, along with armed forces, Serbian ministers, and Russia's ambassador, attended his funeral in Belgrade, which featured military honors and a street procession.
The European Union condemned the military pomp surrounding the funeral, with EU enlargement commissioner Marta Kos cancelling a visit and warning that glorifying war criminals contradicts EU values.
Serbia's government announced it intends to dissolve parliament and hold snap elections following political tensions and recent anti-government anger.

title: Ratko Mladić funeral exposes gap between Serbia’s EU ambitions and political reality
author: Una Hajdari
content:
BELGRADE — Serbia’s hopes of joining the EU were further threatened Monday by the funeral of a notorious army commander convicted of war crimes and the Srebrenica genocide.
Ratko Mladić’s send-off — attended by thousands of people in Belgrade on a balmy September afternoon — drew condemnation from Brussels, which is already at odds with Serbia over its democratic decline, its crackdown on press and judicial freedoms and failure to sanction Russia for the war against Ukraine.
“Any glorification of war criminals, genocide denial and revisionism contradict the most fundamental European values and have no place in the EU or in EU candidate countries,” Christian Wigand, a spokesperson for the European External Action Service, said in a statement Monday, while European Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos canceled a planned visit to Belgrade this week over what she called the “glorification” of Mladić.
summary: Serbia's European Union aspirations face further jeopardy following the large funeral of convicted war criminal Ratko Mladić in Belgrade. The event drew sharp condemnation from Brussels, including a canceled visit by European Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos. This incident adds to existing tensions between the EU and Serbia over democratic backsliding, media freedom crackdowns, and Serbia's refusal to sanction Russia.
key_points: Thousands attended the Belgrade funeral of convicted war criminal and Srebrenica genocide perpetrator Ratko Mladić.
The EU condemned the event, stating that glorifying war criminals contradicts fundamental European values.
European Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos canceled her planned visit to Belgrade due to the glorification of Mladić.
Serbia's EU ambitions are already strained by its democratic decline, restrictions on press and judicial freedoms, and failure to sanction Russia.

title: Flight recorders recovered from 'devastating' Amazon cargo plane crash
author: Jessica Rawnsley
content:
Homendy: 'In the van were seven persons'
- Published
Investigators have recovered the flight recorders from the Amazon cargo plane that crashed at Miami International Airport, but the priority remains the recovery of victims, the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) has said.
Five people were killed and five others seriously injured when the Boeing 767-300, operated by 21 Air, overshot the runway shortly before 14:00 local time (19:00 BST) on Sunday.
The plane hit two vehicles, including a white van carrying seven people within the airport perimeter, and a Toyota with three passengers.
NTSB chairwoman Jennifer Homendy said it was too early to draw conclusions about what caused the crash, with investigators still in the "fact finding stage".
Speaking at a press conference at Miami International Airport on Monday, Homendy said the aircraft had two crew members on board and was arriving from San Juan, Puerto Rico, on its third flight of the day.
The plane struck navigational aids and equipment after overrunning the runway, before hitting a white Ford van owned by a contract cleaning company.
![Tesla cars parked in a lot next to where a crashed Amazon Prime Air cargo plane came to rest](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/999/cpsprodpb/c84c/live/fc526aa0-ab02-11f1-93bd-5b304745dac3.jpg)
It then travelled through a perimeter fence and collided with a Toyota Corolla, coming to rest about 1,300ft (394m) beyond the runway.
Homendy described the crash scene as "devastating", with debris from the aircraft, vehicles and airport fencing scattered across the area.
"It's hard to see, and I'm sure very difficult for the first responders as well," she said.
She said recovering victims' bodies was the current priority, adding: "The investigation and access to the aircraft, as well as evidence, can wait."
The flight data recorder and cockpit voice recorder have been recovered and are being sent to NTSB headquarters for evaluation.
Homendy said investigators could not yet say anything substantive about the cause of the crash as they were still collecting evidence at the scene.
Investigators will examine the flight history, crew experience and training, radar data, and aircraft performance. Separate teams will look at the plane's systems and engines, while a meteorologist will assess the weather conditions at the time of landing.
The NTSB will also examine whether the runway should have had an engineered materials arresting system (EMAS), which is designed to slow and stop aircraft that overrun a runway. Homendy said this would be a "key" part of the investigation.
Earlier analysis by BBC Verify found there was an active thunderstorm near the airport shortly before the crash, with winds gusting up to 26 knots.
The NTSB has appealed for members of the public to share photographs or videos that could aid the investigation.
Homendy said the agency would make safety recommendations at the end of its investigation. "That's why we're here - to prevent the next tragedy," she said.
"Our recommendations must be implemented, or we'll be here again."
Two of the four runways at the airport remained closed following the crash. Passengers have been warned to expect further disruption after Sunday's cancellations affected the arrival of aircraft and flight crews.
The crash happened during the Labor Day holiday weekend, one of the busiest travel periods in the US.
Amazon said it was "heartbroken" by the loss of life and that it was working closely with authorities.
21 Air, the company operating the aircraft, expressed its condolences and said it was co-operating with the investigation.
summary: Investigators have recovered the flight recorders from an Amazon cargo plane that crashed after overrunning the runway at Miami International Airport, resulting in five deaths and five serious injuries. The Boeing 767-300, operated by 21 Air and arriving from San Juan, struck two vehicles, including a van and a Toyota, within the airport perimeter. The National Transportation Safety Board stated that the current priority is recovering victims and that it is too early to determine the cause of the crash.
key_points: Five people were killed and five others seriously injured in the crash.
The flight data recorder and cockpit voice recorder have been recovered for evaluation.
The aircraft overshot the runway and collided with two vehicles inside the airport perimeter.
The NTSB is investigating various factors, including weather conditions, crew experience, and whether an engineered materials arresting system should have been present.

title: German chancellor vows to stay in office despite AfD triumph in state election
author: Deborah Cole
content:
A “shocked” and chastened Friedrich Merz has vowed to stay in office despite the far right’s triumph in a state election that has brought anti-immigrant, pro-Kremlin politicians within striking distance of power.
The German chancellor, appearing ashen-faced in front of reporters in Berlin, said on Monday that the landslide victory by the Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) in Saxony-Anhalt had shaken his conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) “to its very foundations”.
The unpopular Merz, who had pledged to halve the AfD’s support at the national level, has watched the nativist party rack up electoral gains, none as convincing as its utter rout of the CDU in the eastern region on Sunday with nearly 44% of the vote.
The AfD and its candidate Ulrich Siegmund fell short of an absolute majority but could yet create Germany’s first far-right state government since the Nazi period.
Merz appeared contrite and willing to work on his “communication” with voters. “This is the worst electoral defeat the [CDU] has suffered in years, in decades,” he said. “Of course this will have to have consequences.”
Exit polls indicated the state’s voters were driven by deep dissatisfaction with the political establishment and its stewardship of Europe’s biggest economy, with one showing that only 9% approved of Merz’s performance.
![Ulrich Siegmund looks up as he leaves a press conference. He wears an open necked white shirt and stands behind a car as if he is about to get in.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/ae7947f2b2ceba273dcbac20fe01c5fee0199150/0_0_7475_4986/master/7475.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Siegmund, a media-savvy former fragrance salesman, was also able to tap into a sense of grievance in the former communist east, where complaints abound that voters there are treated as “second-class citizens” more than three decades after the fall of the Berlin Wall.
Siegmund, 35, mocked the 70-year-old Merz as “a very good campaigner” for the AfD.
Only 16 months in office, Merz conceded his own low poll ratings had played a role in his party’s loss. “I know that I personally was a constant topic in this election campaign,” he said. “We must try – myself included – to reach people more effectively, in the full range of their emotions.”
The CDU’s junior coalition partner, the Social Democrats, indicated a willingness to water down contentious measures to shore up the statutory healthcare and pension schemes.
However, Merz insisted: “My determination to continue on the path of reform is unbroken,” saying a sustainable system was essential for the sake of “our children and grandchildren”. He added: “Giving up is not an option for me.”
Merz said he wanted to assure Germany’s allies that “our institutions are resilient and stable” and its own vulnerable minorities that the country would stick to its values and constitution even if the AfD took power in Saxony-Anhalt. “We know that Germany carries special responsibility because of its history,” he said.
He also promised to stay the course on Ukraine, stressing he would “not budge a single millimetre from my fundamental conviction that we must defend our freedom against Russia as well”.
Merz said Moscow would cheer the AfD’s success in Saxony-Anhalt and accused it of lending support to the far right’s campaign, with another two German state elections still to come this month amid alleged Russian interference and sabotage.
![Schulze stands holding a microphone in front of a backdrop depicting a tall church or cathedral.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/4ae475f9a574a7a5574684c2afeabed2b39b58db/0_0_5381_3587/master/5381.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Although the CDU rallied behind its chancellor and party leader, several influential commenters openly called for his immediate replacement – a complex step under German law.
after newsletter promotion
Germany “needs a clean slate, a fresh start, and that starts with Friedrich Merz”, said the Der Spiegel editor-in-chief, Dirk Kurbjuweit. “He is evidently the wrong man for this office in these times.”
The AfD’s Saxony-Anhalt chapter is listed as “confirmed rightwing extremist” by the domestic intelligence service. It has pledged mass deportations of unwelcome immigrants and asylum seekers, which critics have said would be illegal, while promising massive boosts in social welfare spending with unclear financing.
The AfD has also taken aim at state support for public broadcasters and cultural institutions it deems “unpatriotic”, sparking fears of “cultural hegemony”.
The party did not win enough seats to elect Siegmund as state premier, but AfD leaders said they seek to pick off rebel lawmakers from other parties willing to play kingmaker. It is only three seats short of a majority.
The conservative-left populist BSW party, which also favours restoring ties with Russia and largely blocking immigration, signalled an openness to working with the AfD but before the election ruled out joining the state government.
In the 13 years of the AfD’s existence, the mainstream parties have maintained a “firewall” against the far right, refusing any formal cooperation that would allow it take power. The strategy meant to sideline the party has appeared to backfire, however, as the permanent “outsider” role appeals to legions of voters fed up with politics as usual.
The CDU state premier, Sven Schulze, acknowledged his party had “no mandate” to govern given its humiliating 17% result, even if it managed to cobble together an unwieldy coalition with all the other parties in the legislature.
Although Saxony-Anhalt forms part of the AfD heartland as a relatively poor, ex-communist region, the party has begun making inroads in the west as well amid alarming signs of decline in the steel, chemicals and automotive sectors.
Germany faces another two regional elections on 20 September, in Berlin and in another eastern state, Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, where the AfD is also strong.
The party co-leader Alice Weidel, beaming after Sunday’s vote, said the AfD was now targeting 40% at the next general election, due in 2029. It is polling at about 28%.
summary: German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has vowed to remain in office despite his Christian Democratic Union suffering a historic defeat in the Saxony-Anhalt state election, where the far-right AfD secured nearly 44% of the vote. Merz acknowledged his own low poll ratings and widespread voter dissatisfaction with the political establishment, but insisted his reform agenda and support for Ukraine will continue. While the AfD fell short of an absolute majority, the party is within striking distance of forming Germany's first far-right state government since the Nazi period.
key_points: The far-right AfD won nearly 44% of the vote in Saxony-Anhalt, routing Chancellor Friedrich Merz's CDU party.
Merz vowed to stay in office and continue his path of reform despite facing calls from some commentators for his resignation.
Voters were largely driven by deep dissatisfaction with the political establishment and stewardship of the economy.
The AfD fell short of an absolute majority but could potentially form Germany's first far-right state government since the Nazi era.

title: World reacts to AfD victory in east Germany state election
author: Al Jazeera Staff
content:
![German Flags are lined up at the venue of the AfD's election party](https://www.aljazeera.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/AFP__20260906__C7GU69V__v1__HighRes__GermanyPoliticsVoteStateSaxonyAnhalt-1788762509.jpg?resize=770%2C513&quality=80)
The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party has won the regional election in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, according to preliminary results.
AfD is set to secure 39 seats at the state parliament in Magdeburg, just short of the 42 seats needed for a majority.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Germans vote in eastern state as far-right AfD eyes power
- list 2 of 3German far-right AfD wins Saxony-Anhalt election, falls short of majority
- list 3 of 3Can AfD form Germany’s first far-right state government since World War II?
The results drew a mixed response around the world, with far-right parties welcoming the news and some governments raising warnings.
Here’s how the world reacted to the news:
French officials
France’s Finance Minister Roland Lescure told RTL radio on Monday that the victory of AfD sends a “very, very worrying signal” to Europe.
He said the continent is facing “a major challenge in the face of a populist wave”, which he says is “spreading around the world today” and that “we must resist [it]”.
France’s European Affairs Minister Benjamin Haddad said the results mark “a very grave moment for Europe” and that “nationalism and xenophobia will never be the answer”.
“We cannot forget our history,” he added.
Santiago Abascal, leader of Spain’s far-right Vox party
“Congratulations, Alice Weidel and Ulrich Siegmund, on this spectacular result, which represents great hope for Germany and Europe,” Abascal wrote on X. Weidel is the AfD’s co-leader, while Siegmund is the AfD’s lead candidate in Saxony-Anhalt.
Andr Ventura, leader of Portugal’s far-right Chega party
Andr Ventura described the result as an “historic victory”.
“Germans are also increasingly opening their eyes to illegal and uncontrolled immigration, corruption and the appropriation of our freedom and identity. Congratulations!” he wrote on X.
Poland’s Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski
Sikorski said the fact that the far-right party narrowly missed a majority was an alarming sign.
“It seems they’re just a few votes short of an absolute majority, but this is indeed a very worrying sign,” he told Radio Vox FM.
Elon Musk
Businessman Elon Musk welcomed the results in a statement on X, simply stating “Gut gemacht!” which translates to “well done” in German.
Siegmund proceeded to personally thank Musk on X for his “support” and “clear and highly important perspective” on the “political developments of our time”.
Former Hungary Prime Minister Viktor Orban
Ex-Prime Minister Viktor Orban called the win “a huge night for Germany and Europe,” and said that “this is just the beginning”.
Former US Ambassador to Germany Richard Grenell
Grenell described the victory as “a huge win and a new day for Germany”, in a statement on X. He also said that “people are ready for change”.
Kirill Dmitriev, CEO of the Russian Direct Investment Fund
Dmitriev said Siegmund was the “voice of reason” in a post on X.
Poland’s Prime Minister Donald Tusk
“In Poland, only idiots or traitors could rejoice the AfD triumph in Germany,” Tusk wrote in a statement on X.
Spain’s Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez
Sanchez said that the “far-right threat” is spreading in Europe and that the German state election result is a “warning” of a bigger political shift, Turkish state news agency Anadolu reported.
“What we saw yesterday in Saxony is a warning, and I think also a confirmation: a warning that the far-right threat, thanks largely to the surrender of the traditional right, is gaining ground in Europe and the world,” he said.
summary: The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party won the regional election in Saxony-Anhalt, securing 39 seats and falling just short of the 42 seats needed for a majority. The election results elicited mixed global reactions, with international far-right figures celebrating the outcome while various government officials and European leaders expressed alarm and warned of a growing populist threat.
key_points: The AfD won the Saxony-Anhalt regional election with 39 seats, just shy of an absolute majority.
French and Polish officials condemned the victory as a worrying signal and a grave moment for Europe.
European far-right leaders, including Spain's Santiago Abascal and Portugal's André Ventura, congratulated the party on its historic success.
Figures such as Elon Musk and former US Ambassador Richard Grenell publicly welcomed the election results on social media.
Leaders like Poland's Prime Minister Donald Tusk and Spain's Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez warned that the far-right threat is gaining ground.

title: Germany's AfD calls for parties to work with it after Saxony-Anhalt win
author: Jessica Parker; Amy Walker
content:
![Ulrich Siegmund, who has greying hair and a short beard and wears a navy suit jacket with a light blue shirt, smiles and waves as he arrives at a press conference on Monday](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/800/cpsprodpb/742c/live/a801c5d0-aa9a-11f1-ab09-7f2415c9a652.jpg)
Ulrich Siegmund, the AfD's leader in Saxony-Anhalt, says the result is a "clear mandate to govern"
- Published
The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) is "very, very close" to taking power, its deputy parliamentary leader has told the BBC, after a historic victory in elections for the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt.
Sunday's preliminary results show it fell three seats short of an outright majority, with 43.8% of the vote. It is now seeking support from other parties or individuals in order to govern.
While most German political parties refuse to work with the AfD, Beatrix von Storch called for its opponents to enter talks and said: "You cannot say I do not accept the vote of the people".
No far-right party has controlled a German state since World War Two, and governing at state level would mean powers over policing and local education.
Von Storch said if parties refused to work with the AfD, "then we might end up in severe chaos and maybe we have a new election".
Her comments were echoed by AfD's leader in Saxony-Anhalt, Ulrich Siegmund, who told a news conference on Monday that the party had won a "clear mandate to govern".
Saxony-Anhalt has a small population of 2.1 million and the AfD in the state is assessed by domestic intelligence as "right-wing extremist", a classification rejected by Siegmund, 35.
Siegmund said discussions with other parties were initiated on Sunday night and could potentially take days or weeks to conclude.
"We reach out to everybody first, we will have consultations and then we'll see whether [there are] individual parliamentary groups or MPs who would be willing to help us," he added.
The AfD is currently heading for 39 seats in the 83-seat state parliament instead of the 42 needed for an outright majority, although the result has not yet been finalised.
Von Storch told the BBC the AfD was talking to individuals within the conservative CDU group - the largest party in both the state's outgoing coalition and Germany's government - because they were "very, very unhappy with their own party".
In Saxony-Anhalt, the CDU won 17.2% of the vote, according to preliminary results.
![Map of eastern Germany highlighting the state of Saxony-Anhalt in white. Key locations marked include Magdeburg (the state capital), Querfurt and Leipzig within or near the highlighted area, and Berlin to the northeast. Poland is shown to the east and the Czech Republic to the south. An inset map in the top right shows the location of Saxony-Anhalt within Germany. A scale bar indicates 50 km and 50 miles. BBC logo in the bottom right corner.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1600/cpsprodpb/cb73/live/5ff40600-a166-11f1-aed2-8d6da8d75094.png)
One idea being floated is whether there could be informal deal whereby a small party - the BSW - could give their tacit support to allow the AfD to form a minority government.
The left-wing populist BSW, which is set to win five seats, is also tough on migration and backs importing Russian gas.
The AfD has signalled an openness to talk with other parties but all - apart from the BSW - refuse to co-operate with the far-right.
The AfD leads the opinion polls nationally, ahead of the ruling conservatives of Chancellor Friedrich Merz and the Social Democrats, but their heartland lies in the eastern states.
They also won the 2024 state election in neighbouring Thuringia, but failed to secure enough seats to win power.
Among the AfD's policies is a highly controversial plan for "remigration", which is widely understood to mean mass deportations of migrants, although the party says it refers to deporting criminals and those in the country illegally.
summary: Following a historic election victory in the eastern German state of Saxony-Anhalt, the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) is calling on other parties to work with it to form a government. The party secured 43.8% of the vote but fell three seats short of an outright majority. While most German parties refuse to co-operate with the AfD, the party is seeking support from individual MPs or other groups such as the left-wing populist BSW.
key_points: The AfD won 43.8% of the vote in Saxony-Anhalt, falling just three seats short of an outright majority.
No far-right party has controlled a German state since World War Two.
AfD leaders are seeking talks with other parties and individual MPs, though most parties currently refuse to co-operate.
The left-wing populist BSW is seen as a potential source of tacit support for a minority government.

title: Europe wrestles with impact of historic regional gains for Germanyâs AfD
author: Katya Adler
content:
![Ulrich Siegmund, leader of the AfD in the state, raises a thumbs up at the election party.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/8c3b/live/72883ac0-aa67-11f1-b26f-b3549bd39fba.jpg)
AfD lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund says the party has won a clear mandate to govern
- Published
"Seismic", "a socio-political earthquake", "a watershed moment for Germany".
This was how political analysts and many media outlets described the stunning victory of the anti-immigration Alternative for Germany (AfD) party in local elections in Germany on Sunday. Is that an exaggeration?
Saxony-Anhalt is one of the smallest of massive Germany's 16 regions. It boasts a mere 1.7m out of 59m eligible voters nationwide. How significant can its political sentiments be, especially since the AfD narrowly failed to win an outright majority?
The answer: very significant.
First and foremost, at home in Germany.
The vote may have been regional but it impacts at national level. The AfD landslide piles even more pressure on the already beleaguered centrist coalition government in Berlin. It may prove to be the nail in the political coffin of Germany's deeply unpopular conservative Chancellor, Friedrich Merz. He had promised to slash the AfD's popularity.
These political woes will further weaken and distract Germany, the EU's most powerful player, at a time of continental crisis - as Europe struggles to contain Russian aggression, Donald Trump's tariff tantrums and the economic threat from China.
The Saxony-Anhalt result also provokes soul-searching throughout Germany, where the Nazi past still looms large. This is the first outstanding electoral landslide for a hard right nationalist party since the fall of the Third Reich in 1945.
The German authorities have labelled the AfD, in part, anti-democratic and a number of regional factions of the party, including Saxony-Anhalt, far right extremist.
The AfD is well known to be particularly popular in east Germany but it's now also polling as the biggest political party nationwide.
Germany's political mainstream has failed voters, it would seem. What does Europe's biggest single economy, its most populous nation not counting Russia, do now?
Tiny Saxony-Anhalt is causing waves outside Germany too.
None other than the President of the United States swiftly posted the Saxony-Anhalt exit poll on his Truth Social platform on Sunday.
The AfD's anti-immigration, anti-woke, "Germany for Germans" message chimes closely with Donald Trump's MAGA missive. Along with a number of other nationalist parties in Europe, the AfD borrows heavily from the Trump playbook - undermining mainstream media, questioning the neutrality of judges and promising to "make Germany great again".
Interesting to note though - the US president is rarely name-checked on the campaign trail in Europe. Politicians are keenly aware just how unpopular he is amongst voters.
Hot on Donald Trump's social media heels on Sunday night was the influential Russian businessman Kirill Dmitriev, CEO of the Russian Direct Investment Fund. He declared the AfD result "historic", Germany's national government "discredited" and the German Chancellor "humiliated", comparing Friedrich Merz to the UK's not-long-gone prime minister, Keir Starmer, who felt forced to resign this summer.
What interest might Russia have in German regional elections, you might ask, and what was Dmitriev's dig at the UK all about?
The German government is the largest single donor to Ukraine and the UK is known to have provided Kyiv with missiles used to strike inside Russian territory. This has deeply angered Moscow.
The AfD, by comparison, is pretty pro-Russia. It wants to stop sending military aid to Ukraine, halt sanctions against Moscow and start buying much cheaper Russian energy again. Energy-hungry German industry suffered a huge economic blow after the country halted Russian energy imports, following the 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
![A crowd waves German flags in front of a stage which has a blue background and AfD's logo.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/7732/live/84a0a430-aa72-11f1-8fb5-49eca7c7c503.jpg)
Crowds waved German flags at the election party after polls closed, where the AfD motto "anything is possible" was displayed
The AfD's softly-softly approach to Russia has another appeal in Germany's east, which remains far poorer than the west. This, despite Germany spending between 2.3 and 3 trillion euros (depending on reports and whether inflation is taken into account) to help integrate the former communist part of the country after the 1989 fall of the Berlin Wall.
Saxony-Anhalt is Germany's poorest region and there, as in much of east Germany, you often encounter what's known as "Ostalgie" amongst voters; essentially "nostalgia in the east" for comparatively more stable times under communism.
Also watching the Saxony-Anhalt election closely was the European Union. The next 12 months is bumper election season across the EU. Ballots are expected in key nations France, Italy, Spain and Poland. Brussels fears more "extreme" parties, left but particularly right of the political spectrum, may benefit across the board.
The leader of Spain's nationalist Vox party, Santiago Abascal, posted on X on Sunday that the AfD victory in Saxony-Anhalt was " a great hope for Germany and for Europe".
By contrast, France's Europe Minister, Benjamin Haddad, an ally of centrist President Emmanuel Macron, warned "this is a serious moment in Europe, seeing the far right win in a regional election in Germany".
Neither the AfD, nor other European parties labelled "extreme right" or "hard right", accept the label. They also differ from one another in tone and party programme. France's National Rally under Marine Le Pen kicked the AfD out of its grouping in the European Parliament two years ago, for being too "radical". What the parties do tend to share, however, is an anti-immigration platform and strong nationalist messaging. And that really worries the EU.
Whether it's a rallying cry for "Germany First" or "Italy First" or "France for the French!", the concern in Brussels is that the rise of nationalist parties strains European cohesion at a time when outside events demand it more than ever.
Nationalist parties like the AfD or Italy's League Party tend to be deeply Eurosceptic, but Brussels says Europe needs to stand united to counter Donald Trump's bullying, for example, or to effectively protect European business against China's goods dumping.
Europe's defence establishment also warns that fractures in European sanctions against Russia or countries going tepid on Nato membership (as you see in Marine Le Pen's National Rally for example, or Germany's AfD) just emboldens Moscow.
Security chiefs say nations must stick together to stop Russia in Ukraine, otherwise the Kremlin will be tempted to attack inside Nato, such as the Baltic states.
The thing is, Europe's voters are very aware of these outside threats and the impact they have at home. They worry about the impact of wars in Ukraine and the Middle East, about crumbling health services at home and dwindling economic security for themselves and their family. Uncontrolled immigration and safety on the streets are huge concerns too.
And this is where the significance of the Saxony-Anhalt vote shines bright. A flashing red warning to traditional political parties, but also to institutions across Europe like the judiciary and security services. Those the AfD dismisses as the self-interested "Establishment".
Voters on this continent feel lost and let down by parties they've supported over and again for decades. Looking right or left now at election time does not mean they've all suddenly become extremist.
The AfD campaign slogan in Saxony-Anhalt was an upbeat "Anything is Possible!" Plus a promise to make Germans feel proud of their country again. Till now untried and untested in government, people seem increasingly willing to give them a go.
  - Published33 minutes ago
 ![Top candidate of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), Ulrich Siegmund, with party co leaders Alice Weidel and Tino Chrupalla, reacts after polls closed, on the day of the Saxony-Anhalt state elections](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/999/cpsprodpb/41a1/live/92680d00-aa0f-11f1-aed2-8d6da8d75094.jpg)
- ![The black of a man wearing a khaki green t-shirt which says 'Deutschland, Meine Heimat' written in a Gothic-style font. The t-shirt shows the insignia of the iron cross](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/770/cpsprodpb/55a5/live/2323ca40-a15b-11f1-92f3-2381193e5eb4.png)
- ![Ulrich Siegmund split picture with BBC Berlin correspondent Jess Parker.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/031a/live/5ff6ef10-aa20-11f1-aed2-8d6da8d75094.jpg)
summary: The anti-immigration Alternative for Germany (AfD) party achieved a historic regional victory in Saxony-Anhalt, marking the first major electoral landslide for a hard-right nationalist party since 1945. This result heaps pressure on Germany's centrist coalition government and Chancellor Friedrich Merz while provoking widespread concern across Europe regarding nationalist gains and EU cohesion. Analysts note the victory reflects growing voter discontent with traditional mainstream parties amid economic and security anxieties.
key_points: The AfD secured a major electoral victory in the regional elections of Saxony-Anhalt, Germany's poorest region.
The result piles pressure on Germany's federal coalition government and Chancellor Friedrich Merz.
The AfD's platform includes halting military aid to Ukraine, lifting sanctions on Russia, and stopping immigration.
The European Union and international observers are concerned that the AfD's rise signals a broader trend of nationalist gains threatening European unity.

title: Flights canceled, airports shut over Indonesia volcanic eruption
author: Associated Press
content:
Indonesia was forced to cancel flights at Jakarta International Airport and service at other domestic airports were also disrupted Sunday when Anak Krakatau volcano erupted, spreading ash across western parts of the country.
Indonesia’s Geological Agency said the volcanic island located in Indonesia’s Sunda Strait between the main Java and Sumatra islands had showed signs of activity since Friday before erupting for 30 seconds at 3:53 a.m. Sunday. Closed-circuit camera footage showed lava flares from the volcano.
No casualties were reported and no evacuation order was issued. The nearest settlement is more than 16 kilometers (10 miles) away, but authorities warned residents and visitors to stay at least 3 kilometers from the active crater.
Volcanic ash spread across parts of Jakarta and Lampung province on Sumatra’s southern tip, Indonesia’s Center for Volcanology and Geological Hazard Mitigation said.
AirNav Indonesia closed airspace around Soekarno-Hatta and Halim Perdanakusuma airports in Jakarta, as well as four other airports, including Radin Inten II Airport in Lampung, because of volcanic ash.
By mid-afternoon, the closure had affected 516 flight movements, with 202 in Jakarta’s Soekarno-Hatta airport alone that affected about 22,800 passengers, on Sunday. The airport was ordered closed until at least 5:30 p.m.
Indonesia’s Directorate General of Civil Aviation said it was closely monitoring the eruption's impact on air travel and coordinating with airlines, airport operators, air navigation services and the meteorology agency.
"Safety remains our top priority in every operational decision,” Lukman F. Laisa, Ministry of Transportation director general of civil aviation, said in a statement.
He warned flight schedules could face cascading disruptions affecting aircraft rotations, fleet availability and terminal capacity as airlines work to restore operations.
The eruption also disrupted services at Bali’s I Gusti Ngurah Rai International Airport and at Medan.
Indonesia’s volcanology agency and the Darwin Volcanic Ash Advisory Centre identified two ash clouds using satellite imagery. One plume rose to 6,100 meters (20,000 feet) and drifted northeast over Jakarta, Banten, West Java and nearby waters.
A second cloud reached 15,200 meters and spread over parts of Banten, Lampung and Bengkulu provinces, the southern Sunda Strait and sections of the Indian Ocean west of Sumatra.
Lana Saria, head of Indonesia’s Geological Agency, said activity at Anak Krakatau has intensified since July, with Sunday’s eruption the strongest during the current period of unrest.
The repeated eruptions indicate a continued supply of magma and volcanic gases beneath the volcano, she said, though officials cannot predict whether a larger eruption will occur.
"We continue to evaluate the volcano’s development based on all monitoring data, not solely on the number of eruptions or the height of the ash column,” Saria said in a video briefing.
She said the main hazards include volcanic ash, high concentrations of gas and the ejection of hot rocks and other material around the crater area.
Anak Krakatau, which means "child of Krakatau," is the offspring of the famous Krakatau, whose monumental 1883 eruption triggered a period of global cooling.
The eruption caused a tsunami in 2018 that killed at least 430 people in Sumatra and Java. Researchers believe volcanic activity triggered an underwater landslide and caused a large chunk of Anak Krakatau’s southwest slope to collapse and displace a large volume of water.
Scientists said Anak Krakatau island was only about a quarter of its original size after that eruption.
summary: The Anak Krakatau volcano in Indonesia erupted on Sunday, sending massive ash clouds into the atmosphere and disrupting air travel across the western part of the country. Authorities canceled flights at Jakarta International Airport and several other regional airports, affecting hundreds of flight movements and tens of thousands of passengers. No casualties or evacuations were reported, though officials maintained a safety perimeter around the crater and warned of potential cascading flight disruptions.
key_points: Anak Krakatau erupted for 30 seconds early Sunday morning after showing increased activity since Friday.
Volcanic ash forced the closure of multiple airports, including major facilities in Jakarta and Lampung, impacting over 500 flight movements.
Two massive ash clouds reached heights of up to 6,100 meters and 15,200 meters, spreading across several provinces and aviation routes.
No casualties or evacuation orders were reported, as the nearest settlement is over 16 kilometers away from the volcano.
Officials noted that Anak Krakatau's activity has intensified since July, indicating a continued supply of magma and volcanic gases.

title: Peace talks rich in symbolism but differences between Russia and Ukraine remain
author: James Landale
content:
![Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskiy, U.S. Special Envoy Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, U.S. President Donald Trump's son-in-law, after a joint news conference,](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/999/cpsprodpb/77dd/live/92218f50-aa29-11f1-a291-b542ee92de7c.jpg)
- Published
The talks in Kyiv were rich in symbolism. The sight of Donald Trump's envoys setting foot on Ukrainian soil for the first time since Russia's full-scale invasion.
The fact they had to travel by train because they could not risk flying and running the gauntlet of Russian drones - weapons launched on the orders of the man at whose table they sat in the Kremlin only hours ago.
The symbolism of Ukrainian President Zelensky greeting Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner at Kyiv's Saint Sophia Cathedral, not only an icon of Ukraine's ancient history, but also just a few yards from where Russian drones hit the headquarters of the country's security services on Friday.
You did not have to join too many dots to work out the point Zelensky was making.
Both sides held talks for several hours; they were later joined by some European national security advisers, including the UK's National Security Adviser Jonathan Powell.
And afterwards, all sides spoke warmly of having held substantive discussions. They spoke hopefully of reviving past "trilateral talks" involving both the US and Europe.
![Russian President Vladimir Putin greets Jared Kushner, U.S. President Donald Trump's son-in-law, and U.S. Special Envoy Steve Witkoff during a meeting at the Kremlin in Moscow, Russia](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/999/cpsprodpb/ae9d/live/c8166d10-aa29-11f1-a291-b542ee92de7c.jpg)
But fundamental differences remain. The US envoys had come hot foot from Moscow where Vladimir Putin had told them Russia was making "tangible advances" on the battlefield.
The story they heard from Ukraine was different, in fact the opposite. Ukrainian officials claim that in August they gained more territory than they lost and Russia suffered 42,000 casualties, dead or wounded.
Putin had also told the US envoys the root causes of the conflict had to be addressed, shorthand for his longstanding strategic demands that Ukraine cede territory, abandon hopes of joining Nato and reduce the size of its army.
After the talks, Zelensky insisted Ukraine would require "strong and clear" security guarantees, including a strong army. Nor did he give any sign of being willing to give up any territory in the eastern Donbas region, an issue he described dryly as "difficult".
Watch: President Zelensky welcomes US envoys in Kyiv
Witkoff insisted progress had been made and the ingredients for a settlement were there.
But he admitted both sides would have to make compromises to narrow the differences between them. And right now, it is hard to see either side doing that.
So for now, the expectation in Kyiv is that the fighting will continue and they will face a hard winter ahead.
Some diplomats talk of a window of opportunity for a possible settlement next spring. Others are less optimistic.
Zelensky thanked the US envoys for their visit because the short-term pause in air strikes agreed by both sides had given the people of Kyiv a brief respite. Few expect it to last for long.
Watch: US envoys Witkoff and Kushner say they are "encouraged" by Ukraine talks
summary: US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner traveled to Kyiv by train to hold substantive peace talks with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and European national security advisers. While the discussions were rich in symbolism and participants spoke hopefully of reviving trilateral talks, fundamental differences remain between Russia and Ukraine. Putin continues to demand territory, the abandonment of NATO ambitions, and a reduced Ukrainian army, whereas Zelensky insists on strong security guarantees and refuses to cede eastern Donbas territory.
key_points: US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner visited Kyiv for peace talks after meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow.
The talks included hours of discussions and involved European national security advisers, such as the UK's Jonathan Powell.
Putin's demands include Ukraine ceding territory, dropping NATO membership hopes, and reducing its army size.
Zelensky insisted on strong security guarantees and indicated unwillingness to give up eastern Donbas territory.
Despite US claims that progress and settlement ingredients exist, both sides face a hard winter with expectations that fighting will continue.

title: Far-right AfD wins vote in Germany’s Saxony-Anhalt state: Exit polls
author: Blow
content:
![Ulrich Siegmund, top candidate in the Saxony-Anhalt state election for the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party AfD's main candidate in the Saxony-Anhalt state election Ulrich Siegmund and the co-leader of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party Alice Weidel celebrate after exit polls following Saxony-Anhalt's state elections at the fairgrounds in Magdeburg, eastern Germany on September 6, 2026. (Photo by Tobias SCHWARZ / AFP)](https://www.aljazeera.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/afp_6a9d968a1172-1788712586.jpg?resize=770%2C513&quality=80)
The Alternative for Germany (AfD) party has won the election in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, according to exit polls, becoming the first far-right party to do so since World War II.
The AfD won 44.5 percent of the vote, exit polls for the ARD broadcaster suggested on Sunday. That is more than twice the 18.5 percent for the incumbent centre-right Christian Democrats (CDU), led by Chancellor Friedrich Merz.
“We have achieved exactly what we wanted to achieve,” said AfD’s lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund. “We have made history in this state.”
AfD co-leader Alice Weidel also hailed a “historic” result, which has given the far-right party a clear mandate to govern, though it was not immediately clear whether it would be able to form a government.
“The reality is the AfD has got the lion’s share of the votes in this election, according to the exit polls. But the question is: is it enough to get them control of the state? Right now, we cannot say for sure,” reported Al Jazeera’s Dominic Kane from Magdeburg in eastern Germany.
Exit polls suggest the party has narrowly missed securing an absolute majority in the state parliament in Magdeburg.
Siegmund said he wanted to extend a hand to all parties willing to bring about a fundamental political transformation in the state. However, the AfD will not bend to other parties’ will, he stressed.
The AfD has never participated in a ruling coalition in Germany’s 16 states nor its federal government, as all other mainstream parties refuse to work with it, a policy infamously known as the “firewall”.
Blow to Merz’s authority
Sunday’s result is another blow to the authority of Merz, whose popularity has declined as his coalition government struggles to revive growth in Europe’s largest economy.
His centre-right CDU came a distant second. Depending on the eventual count, the CDU’s state leader, Sven Schulze, would hope to still be able to form a new multi-party coalition to block the AfD from power.
AfD has tapped into a sense of nostalgia for communist East Germany, as well as lingering resentment about the enduring wealth gap with the west decades after the fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989.
In line with the sometimes defiant sense of local “Ossie pride”, Siegmund has often ridden the iconic local Simson bike, including to the polling booth on Sunday in his hometown of Tangermuende.
While Siegmund has been dubbed the friendly face of the AfD, his campaign promises have been radical, including targeting undocumented migrants with a “remigration and deportation offensive” from day one.
AfD’s agenda
The party’s anti-“woke” agenda also includes promises to replace LGBTQ pride rainbow flags at public schools with the German standard and to change history teaching to lessen the emphasis on Hitler’s Third Reich.
In order to replace migrant workers, the AfD wants to lure back German expatriates, while offering “baby bonuses” for families to reverse the shrinking population in the small state of 2.1 million.
The German Economic Institute has warned that the AfD’s immigration policy would be “ruinous” for Saxony-Anhalt, which is highly reliant on foreign-born workers, especially in the health sector.
Others have voiced fears that an AfD-run state security apparatus could leak sensitive information to Russia, which Moscow could use to destabilise Germany.
The Kremlin “makes no secret of the fact that the AfD is the most important instrument for destabilising Germany for [Russian President Vladimir] Putin,” Thuringia state interior minister Georg Maier told the Handelsblatt daily newspaper.
summary: According to exit polls, the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party has won the state election in Saxony-Anhalt with 44.5 percent of the vote, marking a historic first since World War II. The result deals a significant blow to Chancellor Friedrich Merz, whose centre-right CDU finished a distant second with 18.5 percent. While the AfD secured the largest share of the vote, it narrowly missed an absolute majority, leaving uncertainty over whether it can form a government due to mainstream parties refusing to cooperate.
key_points: The AfD won 44.5 percent of the vote in Saxony-Anhalt, according to exit polls.
The result marks the first time a far-right party has won a German state election since World War II.
Chancellor Friedrich Merz's CDU came in second place with 18.5 percent of the vote.
It remains unclear if the AfD can form a government, as mainstream parties maintain a firewall against working with them.
The AfD's radical platform includes policies targeting undocumented migrants, LGBTQ pride flags, and history curricula.

title: Far-right AfD scores landslide victory in Saxony-Anhalt: exit polls
author: Manuela Scarpellini
content:
If the AfD manages to form a government, it would be the first far-right party to lead a German state since World War II
