The disaster has resulted in a death toll passing 1,000, with thousands still unaccounted for as rescue teams operate in difficult conditions. Specialists attribute the meager response to the dismantling of USAID and its absorption into the state department under the Trump administration. While the state department defended its adaptive and needs-based model, experts argue that former USAID operations would have provided a much faster and more substantial response.
key_points: The US initially announced $500,000 in emergency funds for Nepal floods before raising the contribution to $3.6m.
The flash floods in Nepal have left a death toll exceeding 1,000 with 4,400 people still unaccounted for.
Humanitarian aid specialists criticized the US response as a shadow of its former capacity due to the dismantling of USAID.
The state department defended its response as fast, flexible, and driven by conditions on the ground.
Relief efforts in Nepal are currently being led by neighboring countries India and China.

title: Ukraine war live: Moscow threatens direct strike on Germany as tensions escalate
author: Arpan Rai; Jane Dalton; James Reynolds; Reuters
content:
Russian former president Dmitry Medvedev has threatened Germany with a “direct strike” on military production sites after Berlin accused Moscow of being behind a drone attack on Leipzig Airport last month.
Medvedev, the deputy chair of Russia’s security council and a routinely outspoken provocateur, wrote on Telegram that Germany’s leadership “deserve a direct strike on all German military equipment production facilities ... and quite possibility on several other locations in Berlin as well”.
In an ominous addendum he suggested: “Every terror has sponsors. At the moment, these are the heads of Western countries, primarily European ones. And they often travel to Kyiv by train...”
Workers last month found a drone laden with explosives and a detonator at the airport, which is a base for several Ukrainian cargo planes.
Germany characterises the attempted attack as part of hybrid warfare by the Kremlin meant to cause divisions in countries that back Ukraine. Russia denies involvement.
Chancellor Friedrich Merz has promised President Volodymyr Zelensky that Ukraine will have Germany’s continued support following the discovery.
Russian drones tore into central Kyiv on Wednesday, wounding 11 people on the seventh day running of attacks.
Analysis: Trump doesn’t understand the 'for ever' war he’s created with Iran and Russia
By our world affairs editor Sam Kiley:
Merz says Ukraine can count on Germany after drone attack blamed on Russia
Chancellor Friedrich Merz pledged Germany's continued support for Ukraine in a phone call with President Volodymyr Zelensky, the German government said, following a drone attack at Leipzig airport.
“The chancellor emphasised that Ukraine can count on the resolute continuation of Germany's civilian and military support,” a government spokesperson said.
Mr Merz told Mr Zelesnky about an attempted drone attack at Leipzig Airport last month, for which Berlin says Russia was responsible.
Catch up: Moscow threatens direct strike on Germany in fresh escalation against Europe and UK
Former Russian president Dmitry Medvedev has threatened Germany with a “direct strike” on its military production facilities after Berlin accused Moscow of being behind a drone attack on Leipzig Airport last month.
Medvedev, the deputy chair of Russia’s security council and a regularly outspoken provocateur of the West, wrote on Telegram that Germany’s leadership “deserve a direct strike on all German military equipment production facilities ... and quite possibility on several other locations in Berlin as well”.
In an ominous addendum he suggested: “Every terror has sponsors. At the moment, these are the heads of Western countries, primarily European ones. And they often travel to Kyiv by train...”
Airport workers last month found a drone laden with explosives and a detonator at the airport, an important civilian freight and NATO logistics hub in eastern Germany that is also a base for several giant Ukrainian Antonov An-124 cargo planes.
Germany has blamed Moscow for the attack, characterising it as part of hybrid warfare meant to intimidate and cause divisions in countries that have supported Ukraine over the Russian invasion.
Russia denies involvement and has vowed to respond to what its foreign ministry spokesperson called "anti-Russian action".
Mapped: The UK military bases threatened by Russia as Putin issues ‘military secret’ warning
Vladimir Putin has issued an ominous new warning over the UK’s support for Ukraine saying that it is a “military secret” whether or not Russia is weighing up possible strikes on British military sites.
Last month, Andy Burnham announced that the UK government would release the blueprints for British-made components for the Scalp missile, which is the French version of the UK’s Storm Shadow cruise missile, so Ukraine could produce its own version.
But Russia’s foreign ministry spokeswoman, Maria Zakharova, told Britain to back off on its hostile stance towards Ukraine and said the UK risked taking the conflict to a new level. She told the same Moscow news briefing that Britain and France were "playing with fire" by supplying sensitive missile technology to Ukraine.
See where Britain’s bases across Europe are:
In focus: Why we need to start treating Trump’s America like Russia
Expansionist desires, aggressive military actions, and the consolidation of power in its internal affairs used to attack political enemies, Keir Giles explains how, while writing his new book, he came to realise the two countries are becoming exceedingly hard to tell apart:
Recap: Russian ex-president threatens strike on Germany
Russian former president Dmitry Medvedev has threatened Germany with a “direct strike” on its military production facilities after Berlin accused Moscow of being behind a drone attack on Leipzig Airport last month.
Medvedev, the deputy chair of Russia’s security council and an outspoken provocateur of the West, wrote on Telegram that Germany’s leadership “deserve a direct strike on all German military equipment production facilities ... and quite possibility on several other locations in Berlin as well”.
In an ominous addendum he suggested: “Every terror has sponsors. At the moment, these are the heads of Western countries, primarily European ones. And they often travel to Kyiv by train...”
Airport workers last month found a drone laden with explosives and a detonator at the airport, a Nato logistics hub that is also a base for several Ukrainian Antonov An-124 cargo planes.
Germany blames Moscow for the attack.
Russia denies involvement and has vowed to respond to what its foreign ministry spokesperson called "anti-Russian action".
Russia claims to hit ships supplying weapons for Ukrainian war effort
Russian forces struck two cargo vessels on Wednesday, one in Ukraine's port of Chornomorsk and another in the Black Sea, Russia's Defence Ministry said.
The ministry said the vessels were transporting weapons and ammunition for the Ukrainian military.
It also said Russian forces struck three logistics centres in the Kyiv region and port infrastructure in Odesa. Reuters could not independently verify the ministry's assertions.
On the ground: Russia attacks Kyiv for a seventh consecutive day
Russian drones tore into central Kyiv on Wednesday morning, wounding 11 people and damaging residential and university buildings on the seventh day of nearly round-the-clock attacks that have upended daily life in the city.
The attack on a downtown university took place while students were in class, forcing some 160 to seek shelter, President Volodymyr Zelensky said.
Two people were also killed and eight wounded in Russian strikes on the southeastern city of Dnipro, the regional governor said, where food warehouses and educational buildings were damaged.
It came as Ukraine braces for a new season of Russian strikes on energy infrastructure, amid a critical shortage of US-designed missile interceptors needed to down Moscow's ballistic missiles.
Earlier on Wednesday, Russia struck power facilities in the southern Odesa region with missiles and drones, authorities said, knocking out power to more than 350,000 homes.
Russian President Vladimir Putin said late on Tuesday he had ordered his forces to prepare the new campaign of "massive" strikes.
"Unfortunately, there has been far too little response from the world and its most influential leaders to this latest Russian escalation of strikes," Zelensky wrote on X.
Watch: Putin smirks as he taunts UK over factory attack claims
Ukraine is finalising drone deal with Germany, Zelenskiy says
Ukraine is finalising a drone deal with Germany, president Volodymyr Zelensky said on Wednesday after a call with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz.
The agreement — proposed by Ukraine several months ago — is expected to cover the joint development of various types of drones, missiles and related software.
“Our teams are already finalising the text of the drone deal, and this will, among other things, definitely provide both Germany and Ukraine with additional defence capabilities,” Zelensky said on the Telegram app.
The deal will build on existing German-Ukrainian defence cooperation, including a multi-million-euro programme to supply to Kyiv some 15,000 Strila interceptor drones designed to counter Shahed-type attack drones.
summary: Former Russian president Dmitry Medvedev has threatened Germany with direct strikes on military production facilities following a foiled explosive drone incident at Leipzig Airport, which Berlin attributes to Russian hybrid warfare. Meanwhile, continuous Russian drone and missile strikes have targeted Kyiv, Dnipro, and Odesa infrastructure, injuring multiple civilians and knocking out power to hundreds of thousands of homes. In response to the escalating tensions, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz assured President Volodymyr Zelensky of continued civilian and military support as the two nations finalize a joint defense agreement.
key_points: Dmitry Medvedev threatened a direct Russian strike on German military production facilities and locations in Berlin.
Germany accused Moscow of involvement in an attempted drone attack at Leipzig Airport last month, which Russia denies.
Russian strikes hit central Kyiv, Dnipro, and Odesa infrastructure, wounding multiple people and leaving over 350,000 homes without power.
Chancellor Friedrich Merz pledged continued support to President Volodymyr Zelensky as Ukraine and Germany finalize a joint defense and drone deal.

title: EU and Nato vow to step up pressure on Russia after 'new escalation' in Leipzig
author: Paul Kirby
content:
![European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen (R)and NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte arrive for a press statement at EU headquarters on September 2, 2026](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/819/cpsprodpb/e37a/live/fe3f01b0-a6cb-11f1-b0c9-07afcdd8053c.jpg)
Ursula von der Leyen and Mark Rutte accused Russia of becoming increasingly reckless in its attacks on Europe
- Published
The heads of Nato and the European Commission have warned that Russia is growing increasingly reckless and vowed to respond to a "new normal".
"Leipzig marks a new escalation on European Union soil directly attributed to Russia," said Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, a day after Germany blamed Russia for a failed drone attack last month on Leipzig airport.
"We have to step up and that means being ready to respond to Russia's recklessness faster and better," von der Leyen said. Nato Secretary General Mark Rutte said the whole alliance, which includes the US, stood "in full solidarity with Germany".
Russia has rejected German accusations that a drone carrying explosives deliberately targeted a Ukrainian cargo plane on 4 August.
The drone was defused by a robot at Leipzig/Halle airport and a second drone is thought to have collided with another cargo plane.
A third drone was reportedly found 10 days later at the airport, which is an important Nato hub and is regularly used by Ukrainian Antonov transport aircraft.
It was not until Tuesday that the German government said police investigations and intelligence finding had proved that Russia was behind the incidents.
The interior minister said that the drone's configuration, components, explosives and detonator were all known from other Russian hybrid operations.
Two suspects have reportedly been identified in the Leipzig attack, including a Belarusian with a Russian passport who entered on a tourist visa, and another with Latvian and Russian passports who arrived by plane in Berlin and flew out two days before the failed attack.
![A television reporter films Russian House of Science and Culture shortly after German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul announced Germany's response to the failed drone attack at Leipzig airport September 01, 2026 in Berlin](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/951/cpsprodpb/aadc/live/a18456e0-a6cc-11f1-b0c9-07afcdd8053c.jpg)
The Russian House in Berlin is to close as part of Germany's response to the Leipzig incident
Berlin has said it will close the Russian consulate in Bonn as well as the Russian House cultural institution, widely suspected in Berlin of acting as a propaganda outlet for the Kremlin.
The Russian foreign ministry promised to respond in "mirror-image" fashion and said Berlin had offered no evidence to back its claims. Germany's chargÃ© d'affaires Bernd Finke was summoned to hear Moscow's rejection of Berlin's "entirely unfounded accusations".
Vladimir Putin has condemned Germany's measures as a serious mistake that "clearly runs counter to the interests of the German people".
Asked whether Moscow would be prepared to sever relations with Berlin, Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Alexander Grushko answered "maybe", but said for now it was giving diplomacy a chance.
Critics in Germany suggested the German response was relatively weak, but Berlin has its eye on a more co-ordinated response with its allies, including extended EU sanctions and entry restrictions on Russian visitors across the bloc.
Von der Leyen was clear in her statement that the Leipzig attack had involved "military-grade material carried out by Russian operatives on European Union soil".
"We will not tolerate it," she said.
While she was meeting Rutte in Brussels, EU foreign ministers had gathered at Wicklow in Ireland, where France's Foreign Minister Jean-NoÃ«l Barrot said action could be taken on a European level against Russia's so-called "shadow fleet" of ships carrying oil and other cargo aimed at avoiding EU sanctions.
Barrot and fellow ministers from Belgium and the Netherlands said they had summoned Russian ambassadors in protest at the attack.
Lithuania's Foreign Minister Kestutis Budrys said it was obvious that Russia saw no political cost in its hybrid operations against European allies.
EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said they were working on how to tighten enforcement of existing sanctions, and added there was broad support for an EU visa entry ban on Russian ex-combatants as well as stricter visa limits on Russian tourists.
Several EU countries, including Sweden, the Netherlands, Poland and Spain, are pushing for more than â¬193bn (Â£165bn) in frozen Russian assets to be used to help Ukraine. The idea was first planned at the end of 2025, and rejected by Belgium where the money is held. However, Belgium's position is unchanged because it fears being held financially liable by the courts.
The Leipzig attack was part of a broader pattern of increasingly dangerous incidents, including drones and interference with critical infrastructure, von der Leyen said.
Mark Rutte added there had been increased risk to Europeans from drones and missiles crossing into countries on the Alliance's eastern flank, and there had been more "malign activities targeting our territory directly, whether it is fires set in factories producing defence equipment for Ukraine or indeed the Russian hybrid attack in Leipzig".
![German police secures the area after a second sabotage attempt on Germany's electricity grid, with local police saying they are investigating an attack on a substation in Bergheim, Germany, September 2, 2026](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/999/cpsprodpb/b3a4/live/59ba3230-a6cc-11f1-aed2-8d6da8d75094.jpg)
Police search an area in Bergheim after an attack on a substation
Several acts of suspected sabotage have been reported in Germany in the past 24 hours alone, including two attacks on electricity substations, one in the east and one in the west near Cologne.
Although authorities do not yet know who was behind the incidents, North Rhine-Westphalia Interior Minister Herbert Reul said an attack that targeted power lines at Bergheim in western Germany was deliberate and whoever had carried out was attacking the country as a whole.
"We are investigating two possibilities: sabotage directed by a foreign state and left-wing extremism," he said.
Several power lines failed prompting five power plant units to go offline at two separate coal-fired power stations. Police said six launching devices had been found in a field.
High-voltage power lines were damaged near the JÃ¤nschwalde coal-fired power plant in Brandenburg early on Tuesday and explosive devices were later found at a substation.
Meanwhile, in neighbouring Poland, Prime Minister Donald Tusk said a fire at a factory producing combat drones at SkarÅ¼ysko-Kamienna, 140km (85 miles) south of Warsaw was a deliberate act of arson and sabotage. Arson has also not been ruled out in a fire at a factory in Lublin on Sunday night.
Von der Leyen said sanctions had already been used to deter Russia, and EU foreign ministers were discussing further ways of "cutting deeper in Russia's war chest".
The EU has already agreed to loan Ukraine â¬90bn (Â£77bn), and von der Leyen said Kyiv had asked for billions of extra euros in funding to help pay for PAC-3 air defence missiles. Work was already taking place on a joint Europe-Ukraine Freyja anti-ballistic missile defence project, she added.
She promised that Europe and Nato would just maintain pressure on Moscow but "we will increase it and we will not stop, not until Russia stops bombing and killing innocent children, men and children in Ukraine".
summary: The heads of the EU and NATO have vowed to increase pressure on Russia following a failed drone attack on Leipzig airport, which Germany attributed to Russian operatives. In response to the incident and other recent infrastructure sabotage, Germany has ordered the closure of a Russian consulate and a cultural institution, while EU ministers discuss further sanctions and visa restrictions. Russia has rejected the accusations as unfounded and promised a mirror-image response.
key_points: European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte condemned Russia for escalating hybrid operations on European soil, specifically citing a failed drone attack at Leipzig airport.
Germany blamed Russia for the attack, identifying suspects and responding by closing the Russian consulate in Bonn and the Russian House cultural center in Berlin.
Russia rejected the allegations as entirely unfounded and stated it would respond in a mirror-image fashion.
EU foreign ministers are considering broader retaliatory measures, including stricter visa limits on Russian tourists, enforcement of existing sanctions, and targeting Russia's shadow fleet.
Authorities are also investigating additional recent infrastructure incidents in Germany and Poland, including suspected sabotage on electricity substations and factory fires.

title: USS Abraham Lincoln arrives at Thai port after gruelling 270 days at sea
author: Natasha May
content:
The USS Abraham Lincoln, a US aircraft carrier at the centre of a row over conditions on board after months at sea as part of Donald Trump’s war against Iran, has arrived off a Thai port.
Reports of deteriorating living conditions and poor mental health on the vessel, including attempted suicides, have made headlines around the world, provoking criticism of the president’s actions in the Middle East.
A heavy security presence was in force at Laem Chabang port near Pattaya, south of Bangkok, where the 5,000-strong crew of the USS Abraham Lincoln arrived on Wednesday morning after more than 270 days at sea.
The huge nuclear-powered ship left California in November 2025 for duty in the South China Sea and was rerouted to the Middle East before US-Israeli attacks on Iran that began six months ago.
The resort city of Pattaya, a rest-and-recreation destination for US troops since the Vietnam war, has stepped up security as it prepares to welcome the sailors and Marines.
![A tug boat greets the USS Abraham Lincoln as it arrives at the port in Laem Chabang, Chonburi, Thailand.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/e6670588d69f95fd51e3bb3369815a758218a78e/72_83_5283_3487/master/5283.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
The sailors will disembark in groups of approximately 50, according to police colonel Anek Srathongyoo, a superintendent of Pattaya city police station.
Once a quiet fishing village, Pattaya was transformed into one of the most infamous red light districts in the world with the arrival of American troops using military bases in Thailand during the Vietnam war.
At its peak, tens of thousands of US military personnel came through each year, said Pipatpong Fakfare, an associate professor specialising in tourism at Bangkok University.
“In my opinion, it’s really the founding influence for the town. The US military turned a quiet fishing village into a global destination for an international nightlife and entertainment hub in about 15 years,” he said.
Pattaya is now hugely popular with foreign tourists, known for its beaches and a nightlife scene that has long drawn scrutiny over sex tourism.
Although the American troops left by the mid-70s, the sex industry infrastructure continued to grow, with European tourists taking their place, and more recently waves of Chinese and Russian visitors, Pipatpong said.
![The USS Abraham Lincoln](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/cdad8c481e0f275d8c5c4e2d1199fa297ca4932d/343_440_6109_4002/master/6109.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Sex work is illegal in Thailand, but authorities often turn a blind eye, said Pattarachit Gozzoli, a sociologist at Mahidol University in Bangkok.
Pattaya’s mayor, Poramase Ngampiches, has downplayed the city’s past, saying there had been a recent crackdown on sex workers but denied it was linked to the US arrivals. Local police arrested 25 women for soliciting on the beachfront promenade a week before the ship arrived.
The mayor said buses had been arranged to transport the sailors between the ship and Pattaya until the carrier departs on Sunday.
Outside one bar, a sign said: “Welcome all US military personnel. Thank you for your service.”
Poramase said in a Facebook post: “They come to relax. Our preparations will focus on safety and ensuring fair pricing, so we don’t take advantage of them.”
He said they had been banned from water sports such as jetskis, and from taking advantage of Thailand’s lax cannabis laws, but encouraged them to enjoy the city’s many other attractions, from malls to religious sites.
summary: The USS Abraham Lincoln has arrived at a Thai port near Pattaya after spending more than 270 days at sea amid reports of deteriorating living conditions and poor mental health among its 5,000-strong crew. The nuclear-powered carrier's deployment followed a rerouting to the Middle East for duty related to US-Israeli actions against Iran. Local authorities and businesses have increased security and prepared the resort city to host the sailors for rest and recreation until the ship departs on Sunday.
key_points: The USS Abraham Lincoln arrived at Laem Chabang port in Thailand after more than 270 days at sea.
The 5,000-strong crew's lengthy deployment and reports of poor mental health and living conditions have drawn global headlines.
Pattaya authorities implemented heightened security measures and arranged transport for sailors disembarking in groups.
Sailors were banned from water sports and Thailand's legal cannabis, but encouraged to visit local malls, religious sites, and attractions.

title: Nepal floods: Father borrows $13, walks for days to search for missing son
author: Smita Sharma
content:
![Talka Sada, backpack on his shoulders, is trekking across Nepal's flood-hit areas, searching for his missing son. \[Smita Sharma/ Al Jazeera\]](https://www.aljazeera.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Talka-Sada-1788329553.jpeg?resize=570%2C380&quality=80)
Kathmandu/Nuwakot, Nepal — Talka Sada’s eyes are exhausted, the wrinkles on his face deep with worry. His heels hurt after walking long miles across Nepal’s mountains. He’s hungry and angry, but as his mood shifts between hope and helplessness, his focus remains on his mission: a desperate search for his son.
Sada, who is in his 50s, is from Saptari, a district in Nepal’s Terai region — the plains that stretch across southern Nepal, south of the Shivalik Hills and north of the porous border with India.
People from this part of the Himalayan nation are known as Madhesis, a distinct ethnolinguistic population with a diverse regional, cultural and caste identity. Vinod, his only son — Sada also has three daughters — has been missing since the devastating flash floods of August 26 destroyed homes, schools, bridges, power plants and everything in their path in large parts of northern Nepal.
Sada last spoke to 19-year-old Vinod a day before the floods that grew from the Bhotekoshi river. Vinod had come to the Rasuwa district, the region worst affected by the floods, a month earlier to work as a labourer at a hydropower plant. He would mix cement and take on other odd jobs. Four other young men who worked with him — all between 17 and 19 years old — are also missing since the floods.
“I can’t tell you how much my wife is howling. I am in deep pain myself and I do not know what to do,” Sada says as he wipes his tears.
![Talka Sada, right, and his brother, are searching for Sada's son, who has been missing since the August 25 floods that devastated large parts of northern Nepal \[Smita Sharma/ Al Jazeera\]](https://www.aljazeera.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Talka-Sada-2-1788329610.jpeg?w=640&resize=640%2C410&quality=80)
Search, trek, search again
Dressed in a faded white shirt and black pants, the father wears an orange polythene bag as a raincoat. He carries a grey backpack on his shoulders. With him is his brother, Sada’s companion on a long and increasingly frustrating journey.
Sada shows a dirty handkerchief in his pocket with notes amounting to less than 2,000 Nepali rupees (about $13) crumpled in it. It’s money he borrowed to be able to crisscross Nepal’s flood-affected areas in search of his son.
“I borrowed money to come all the way from Saptari to here. I have to pay an interest of 20 rupees on every 100 rupees I have borrowed,” he says. The brothers used some of that money to take a bus from Saptari to the national capital, Kathmandu. That 292km (181-mile) journey takes nine hours because of Nepal’s hilly terrain.
In Kathmandu, Sada and his brother went from hospital to hospital to look for Vinod among survivors or in the list of those declared dead — many of the flood victims were flown into Kathmandu from the northern parts of Nepal.
Outside mortuaries, the photographs displayed are often difficult to recognise. Most bodies being retrieved are decomposed or dismembered. There was no sign of Vinod — nor his name or photo at the hospitals.
So, Sada started walking towards Nuwakot (nearly 60km away from Kathmandu), closer to the location of the hydropower plant where his son was believed to be working.
After a gruelling, hours-long walk through broken roads, they reached Trishuli, a town on the way whose market now lies covered with debris, mud and slush.
“Last night when we reached here, a lodge charged us 1,500 Nepali rupees to stay the night. They gave us only one small serving of rice that did not even satisfy our hunger,” says Sada. “Now if we have to stay here another night, all my remaining money will finish and I will be left with nothing to go back home.”
![Nepal army soldiers work during a search and rescue operation outside a tunnel near the Hydropower Project sites, following deadly flash floods and mudslides, in Rasuwa district, Nepal, in this handout obtained by Reuters on September 1, 2026. Nepal Army/Handout via REUTERS THIS IMAGE HAS BEEN SUPPLIED BY A THIRD PARTY. MANDATORY CREDIT. NO RESALES. NO ARCHIVES.](https://www.aljazeera.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/reuters_6a96895f-1788250463.jpg?w=770&resize=770%2C433&quality=80)
‘They are pushing us away’
Sada and his brother say they just want access to mortuaries and army camps set up to help evacuate survivors and take bodies from the disaster zone, but claim that he has been turned away repeatedly.
To the brothers, the response they’ve received to their pleas for help is a product of deep-seated ethnic and caste divisions within Nepal. Madhesis — as the people of the Terai are known — have long accused the hills-based Nepali elite of discriminating against them.
Sada’s family is from the Musahar community, a particularly marginalised community that lives in the Terai and in the Indian states of Uttar Pradesh and Bihar.
“We are poor. They think of us as Madheshis and Biharis. We cannot speak Nepali fluently — which is why they are just pushing us away and making us run from pillar to post,” Sada claims, as he sobs. “Even if it is a corpse, we have a right to see it. We have registered our names everywhere – police stations to military camps. But no one is helping us.”
Nepali authorities, overwhelmed by the scale of the crisis — more than 1,000 people have been killed, and thousands are still missing — insist they are trying their best to reach and help all survivors.
![Nepal's army personnel carry the bodies of deceased flood victims during a search operation along the Narayani river at Bharatpur in Nepal's Chitwan district on August 31, 2026. Nepal was burying on August 31 some of the hundreds of bodies retrieved after a deadly, tsunami-like flood crashed through the Himalayan region, sweeping away villages and leaving thousands still missing. (Photo by PRAKASH MATHEMA / AFP)](https://www.aljazeera.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/AFP__20260831__C6VZ6KR__v1__HighRes__NepalDisasterFlood-1788169144.jpg?w=770&resize=770%2C513&quality=80)
Helplessness and anger
The brothers try dialling Vinod’s phone number for the umpteenth time, but get no response. “We can’t talk to him. We don’t hear his voice. So everyone is heartbroken back home,” says Sada. “My wife asked me to get our son back. So we are searching all hydropower plants, but where do I find him?”
One minute, Sada is hoping for a miracle. “My son is young. He is a porter. He is daily wager. So he is agile. He could have surely walked, ran somewhere,” he wonders.
The very next moment, though, the father’s voice rings with helplessness. “I have no hope,” he says. “If Vinod was alive, he surely would have called from somewhere, even if he went to drink water.”
Yet giving up isn’t an option — not yet, at least.
So, Sada and his brother prepare to continue their trek towards the power plant where Vinod worked. As they leave, the father issues a warning that rings with a sense of betrayal and anger.
“We will have to burn down the police station if no one answers or helps us,” he shouts.
summary: Talka Sada has borrowed money and is trekking across Nepal's flood-hit areas to search for his 19-year-old son, Vinod, who has been missing since devastating flash floods on August 26. Vinod was working as a laborer at a hydropower plant in the severely affected Rasuwa district when the disaster struck. Sada and his brother have searched hospitals, mortuaries, and disaster zones, but claim they are being ignored and discriminated against due to their Madhesi identity. Meanwhile, Nepali authorities state they are overwhelmed by a crisis that has killed more than 1,000 people and left thousands missing.
key_points: Talka Sada's 19-year-old son, Vinod, went missing following catastrophic flash floods in northern Nepal on August 26.
Sada borrowed less than 2,000 Nepali rupees (about $13) at high interest to fund his search journey across flood-affected regions.
Vinod was one of five young migrant laborers working at a hydropower plant in the Rasuwa district who vanished during the floods.
Sada alleges that marginalized Madhesis face discrimination and lack of assistance from authorities in their search efforts.
Nepal's authorities report being overwhelmed by the disaster, which has caused over 1,000 deaths and left thousands missing.

title: Iran attacks US bases in Middle East after reports US strike killed five at wedding party
author: Joe Coughlan; Claire Keenan
content:
![Several ships sit in a large body of water, with fog on the horizon and blurred rocks in the foreground.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/999/cpsprodpb/913b/live/5a3308c0-a629-11f1-a291-b542ee92de7c.jpg)
Vessels were visible across the Strait of Hormuz from Oman this week
- Published
Tehran has launched missile and drone attacks at US targets in Jordan, Kuwait, Iraq and Bahrain after American forces resumed strikes against Iran on Tuesday.
The Iranian Red Crescent reported five people, including a child, were killed and more than 50 injured when shrapnel from a US missile attack hit a home where a wedding celebration was taking place in Sirik in southern Iran.
The US military said it was aware of the reports but that it never targeted civilians.
US Central Command (Centcom) said US strikes on Iran followed "recent attempted attacks" by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) against commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and American forces in the region.
The IRGC said the US would "regret" the strikes. By early Wednesday, it had launched a barrage of ballistic missiles at a US Marine base in Jordan's Aqaba in retaliation for the Sirik attack, according to Iran's semi-official Tasnim news agency.
The Jordanian Armed Forces said it had intercepted 13 ballistic missiles, 10 of which were destroyed, while three fell in remote areas. There were no deaths or injuries as a result of the attack from Iran.
The network also said that the country's national security centre had warned residents of the Aqaba and Mafraq governorates of falling debris, adding that the warning had since ended.
Separately, the Kuwait army said its air defences were responding to Iranian missile attacks early Wednesday.
Several explosions were also reported in Bahrain following attacks by Iran, according to Iranian state media.
In Iraq's autonomous Kurdistan region, Iran's Revolutionary Guards said on Wednesday they had struck US bases with missiles and drones, destroying a maintenance centre, warehouses and equipment, state-run IRNA reported.
Donald Trump, when the US strikes were announced on Tuesday afternoon, warned that Iran would be hit again at "a much harder and higher level" if it retaliated.
The attack follows the first known US strikes on Iran since late July earlier this week, when forces attacked two rocket launchers on Larak Island in the strait. Tehran retaliated by firing missiles at air bases in Jordan and a drone at the UAE.
Centcom said US forces had begun striking IRGC targets at 12:00 ET (16:00 GMT), and had completed the strikes by early Wednesday.
Iranian state media reported projectiles had hit the areas of Chabahar and Konarak and an airport in Jiroft, and that explosions were heard in Qeshm island and Bandar Abbas.
US Navy Captain Tim Hawkins, speaking on behalf of Centcom, told the BBC it was aware of reports from Iranian state media of the attack in Sirik.
He added: "The US military never targets civilians, unlike the IRGC."
![Map of Strait of Hormuz](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1600/cpsprodpb/bd5e/live/88ae2b00-a631-11f1-a291-b542ee92de7c.png)
The US and Israel launched wide-ranging strikes on Iran on 28 February, with Iran responding by attacking Israel, US bases and allied states in the Gulf, and effectively closing the Strait of Hormuz to marine traffic.
A US-Iran agreement, known as the Memorandum of Understanding, to extend a ceasefire between the two countries was signed in June.
However that agreement has expired, leading to a resumption of hostilities. Both the US and Iran have also fired on shipping, with Tehran targeting vessels it says have sought to cross the strait without its permission and the US enforcing a naval blockade of Iranian ports.
Washington also announced a fresh sanctions campaign on 24 August aimed at further isolating Tehran and expanding secondary sanctions against its allies.
Speaking at a G20 finance ministers meeting, the US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said many US allies "came forward and said they will do whatever is necessary" concerning the sanctions against Iran.
Iranian officials and state media have largely dismissed the campaign as a continuation of previous US economic measures, which they argue followed Washington's military failure in the recent conflict.
However, on Tuesday Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian was quoted by state media as saying if the US returned to committing to the agreement, Iran would reciprocate.
summary: Iran launched missile and drone attacks targeting US bases in Jordan, Kuwait, Iraq, and Bahrain following resumed American military strikes. The escalation occurred after reports that a US missile strike in Sirik killed five people at a wedding party, though the US military stated it never targets civilians. The hostilities follow the expiration of a US-Iran ceasefire agreement and ongoing tensions in the Strait of Hormuz.
key_points: Iran launched ballistic missiles and drones at US targets in Jordan, Kuwait, Iraq, and Bahrain.
The Iranian Red Crescent reported five people were killed when a US missile attack hit a home during a wedding celebration in Sirik.
The US military stated it was aware of the reports but emphasized that it never targets civilians.
Jordanian armed forces intercepted 13 ballistic missiles with no resulting deaths or injuries.
Hostilities resumed following the expiration of a US-Iran ceasefire agreement and recent attempts to target commercial shipping.

title: US launches new airstrikes on Iranian targets as hostilities flare
author: Lucy Campbell
content:
The US launched new airstrikes on Iranian targets on Tuesday, quashing hopes that an exchange of fire last weekend might not presage a wider renewal of hostilities.
Oil prices had already risen after that first exchange of direct attacks since July and after reports of two tankers being hit leaving the strait of Hormuz, the global oil supply waterway that Iran has effectively closed to shipping.
Tehran remained defiant, warning that it would prevent oil being exported from the Gulf, despite a threat by Donald Trump to hit Iran “hard” in response to the renewed Iranian strikes, and a warning from Scott Bessent, the US treasury secretary, that Washington was about to impose new sanctions.
“Today at 12 p.m. ET (1600 GMT), U.S. forces began striking Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) targets in Iran,” US Central Command posted on X. “The strikes follow recent attempted attacks by the IRGC against commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and against American service members deployed to the region.”
Iran’s state broadcaster said there had been reports of explosions on Iran’s Qeshm Island, on the northern side of the strait.
The state-linked news agency Nour News said there had been reports of explosions in the port city of Bandar Abbas and in Chabahar, a port on the southern coast.
The six-month conflict had shifted into an economic standoff before the weekend strikes, in which US forces attacked Iran’s Larak Island on Sunday and Iran responded by launching missiles at two US airbases in Jordan.
Although he warned of a US response to the Iranian strikes, the US president also told reporters on Monday that they did not signal a return to full-scale war, and a senior Iranian source told Reuters they were a “limited and contained confrontation”.
However, Trump made dire threats against Tehran on social media. He warned that if Iran retaliates against the US’s latest strikes, “they will be hit again at a much harder and higher level, but it will not be the biggest attack of them all, that is waiting in the wings and, when it is over, there will be very little left of the Islamic Republic of Iran”.
The ominous last part of Trump’s message was starkly reminiscent of threats the US president has made in the past that could amount to war crimes if carried out, including threatening to destroy critical civilian infrastructure such as power plants and bridges, threatening to bomb Iran “back to the Stone Ages”, and an April threat that “a whole civilization will die tonight” if a peace deal wasn’t reached.
In Iran, the Fars news agency quoted an IRGC spokesperson as saying the US “will regret its new attacks”.
The IRGC later said it had begun a “regretful response to the aggressors” amid the fresh US attacks on southern Iran, state broadcaster IRIB reported.
In its statement, the IRGC said that “in blind and desperate attacks”, the US had bombed several locations, including civilian areas. It went on: “Attacks that tightened the blockade of the strait of Hormuz and strengthened the determination of the fighters to suppress the foreign forces interfering in the strait of Hormuz. The brave warriors of the IRGC have begun a regretful response to the aggressors, and in the first action, using the new aerospace defence system, they shot down the 50th advanced MQ9 drone of the invading American army.”
Recent pledges by both sides to respond to further attacks have highlighted how quickly a conflict that has increasingly been fought through sanctions, blockades and economic pressure could spill back into military action.
Masoud Pezeshkian, Iran’s president, had said early on Tuesday that Tehran would reciprocate immediately if Washington honoured its commitments under a June memorandum of understanding (MOU) that was intended to halt the conflict.
The MOU declared an end to fighting that has now killed thousands in Iran and Lebanon since US and Israeli strikes began on 28 February. But it also deferred many of the most difficult issues and paved the way for a broader 60-day negotiation period – which passed without further agreement.
“I am stating clearly that if the US returns to its commitments under the memorandum of understanding, the Islamic Republic of Iran will immediately reciprocate,” Pezeshkian said in the Kyrgyz capital, Bishkek, at a summit of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation, which includes Russia and China.
But Iranian officials have shown no public sign of bowing to pressure.
“If the enemy wants us not to export oil from the Persian Gulf, no one will be able to export oil,” Mohammad Baqer QalibafIran’s parliament speaker was quoted as saying by Iranian media. If the US intensified its “siege”, he said Tehran would respond militarily.
Esmaeil Baghaei, Iran’s foreign ministry spokesperson, told a press conference in Tehran that Washington was “addicted to making excessive demands and has mistaken negotiations for dictating terms”.
“As long as they act in this manner, they will certainly get no result other than what they have achieved so far,” he added, warning that Tehran would “use all our capabilities, whether on the battlefield or through our diplomatic apparatus”.
Reuters contributed reporting
summary: The United States launched new airstrikes against Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps targets in Iran on Tuesday following attempted attacks on commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and American service members. The fresh military action dashed hopes that a previous weekend exchange of fire would not lead to renewed hostilities, causing oil prices to rise amid Iranian threats to block oil exports from the Gulf. While both sides exchanged warnings of severe retaliation and military escalation, the six-month conflict continues to feature a mix of economic blockades, sanctions, and direct military clashes.
key_points: US forces began striking IRGC targets in Iran on Tuesday following attacks on commercial shipping and American service members.
Explosions were reported in Iranian locations including Qeshm Island, Bandar Abbas, and Chabahar.
President Donald Trump threatened severe retaliation if Iran responds to the latest US strikes.
Iran's IRGC claimed to have begun a response to the aggression, stating it shot down an American MQ9 drone.
Iranian officials warned that Tehran would prevent oil exports from the Gulf if the US intensifies its siege.

title: Germany blames Russia for drone attack at Leipzig airport
author: Kate Connolly
content:
The German government has blamed Russia for the drone attack on Leipzig airport last month, calling it “dangerous behaviour” and part of a systematic and concerted effort by Moscow to “cause great damage” through a large number of hybrid attacks.
The interior minister, Alexander Dobrindt, and the foreign minister, Johann Wadephul, ended weeks of speculation and the government’s hesitancy to blame Russia, saying in a brisk 10-minute briefing in Berlin that all indications were the Russian state had provided the knowhow and equipment for the planned attack and “low-level agents” were recruited to carry it out.
A drone loaded with explosives was discovered at Leipzig/Halle airport on 4 August attached to the wing of a Ukrainian Antonov cargo plane used to transport weapons to Ukraine. It failed to detonate but could have caused a catastrophe, authorities said.
Russia will face a package of penalty measures, Wadephul said, adding that the German government saw “a need for appropriate and necessary action in this situation”. It would respond “to this hybrid attack in Leipzig with proportionate and measured, yet equally resolute, action”, he said. “We are not at war, but we are a daily target of hybrid warfare.”
He added: “The dangerous behaviour of the Russian Federation is part of attempts at destabilisation, disinformation, threats, sabotage and aggression.” Berlin regretted the abysmal state of its relations with Moscow, he said.
![Germany’s foreign minister, Johann Wadephul, speaking at a press briefing](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/c1eb6fa3d829bd6e6bb29cc95bb57e8da2518ec4/389_140_3158_2527/master/3158.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
The EU expressed “full solidarity” with Germany over the attack, and Nato assured Berlin that it would defend its members.
The Russian ambassador had been summoned to the foreign ministry at that very moment to be informed of the consequences, Wadephul said. The Russian consulate in Bonn will be closed later this month, and Russian House, a sprawling cultural and science institute in the centre of Berlin, which is alleged to house Russian spies and to have been the launchpad for a number of hybrid attacks carried out in Germany over the past few years, is to be turned out of its rented building.
A clampdown on Russia’s shadow fleet – illegal ships carrying Russian oil and other supplies in the Baltic and North seas – is also planned. Sweden and Finland track and disrupt the shadow fleet but Germany does not, so vessels regularly opt to sail via German waters in its foreign economic zones.
New lists of people on a blacklist would be drawn up and tighter border controls of Russians entering Germany would be carried out, Wadephul said.
Parallel to these moves, Berlin is also backing the European Commission’s 22nd package of sanctions, to cover a further 1,600 companies and organisations with a Russian connection.
Responding to Germany’s announcement, Russia’s foreign ministry spokesperson, Maria Zakharova, said Moscow would respond to what she called Berlin’s “anti-Russian action”, according to the Interfax news agency.
The government has previously said it does not intend to directly involve Nato by invoking article 4 of the alliance. However, its Nato and European partners were informed about the investigation and agreed on the planned consequences, Wadephul confirmed.
The Nato secretary general, Mark Rutte, and the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, promised “full solidarity” with Berlin.
Rutte said Berlin had put forward clear evidence of Moscow’s role in the “hybrid attack” and welcomed the measures announced in response, while von der Leyen vowed to “keep the EU united despite these escalating and serious acts”.
![Police officers walk across a field at the airport](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/905e68e9072ad94a0fada6f94806012c003dc6fe/0_0_4096_2730/master/4096.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Tuesday’s announcement marks the first time the German government has concretely named Russia as responsible for the attack.
It marks the lowest point in decades for relations between Russia and the EU’s largest member, which had already plunged after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
This weekend will see a critical election in the eastern states of Saxony-Anhalt and Mecklenburg Vorpommern, in which the war in Ukraine and relations with Russia have been a focal point.
The far-right populist Alternative für Deutschland, which is pushing a pro-Russia agenda as it seeks to win an absolute majority in Saxony-Anhalt, has accused the government of double standards over its treatment of Russia. Urging the government to prove Russia’s involvement in the Leipzig incident earlier this week, it said the same rigour should be applied to investigations into the attack on the Nord Stream pipeline, for which Ukraine is alleged to have been responsible.
![Wrapped freight on mobile pallets under a plane in Ukraine colours with the legend 'Be brave like Kherson'](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/90fab552e833c01fd5c9dd7ef906baf55dbb0c00/247_0_1156_925/master/1156.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
The drone in the Leipzig incident was carrying 600g of explosives and was discovered in the security area of the airport close to Ukrainian Antonov cargo planes on the night of 4-5 August. The explosive device detonator appeared to have failed. A second drone was believed to have been part of the planned attack but investigators have since thrown doubt on that theory. Traces of the military explosive hexogen were found on the edge of the airport on 14 August along with a further drone, investigators confirmed. Had the devices exploded they could have caused a catastrophe, German officials said.
The chancellor, Friedrich Merz, who last week said whoever was behind the attack “will pay”, did not attend the briefing to the press and public on Tuesday.
Konstantin von Notz, the Green party’s security policy expert and commissioner for intelligence oversight, criticised the government before the announcement for what he described as its failure to stand up to Vladimir Putin in the face of the growing hybrid threat from Russia. “The federal government must finally stop being hesitant, reticent and timid. Things must be called by their name, and decisive action must be taken,” he said in an interview with the RND network.
Even within his own Christian Democratic Union party, Merz has faced calls to be tougher towards Russia. On Tuesday, the party’s foreign policy expert, Roderich Kiesewetter, urged the chancellor to take a tougher line against Russia, accusing successive governments of exercising “extreme caution with regard to Russian state terrorism on German soil”.
Citing sources in German intelligence, Bild Zeitung said direct connections had been made by investigators between other drone and explosives finds and incidents in Germany and across Europe, including in Romania, Italy, Poland, Bulgaria and the UK. A cache of weapons discovered recently in a Berlin forest are thought to be connected to Russian activities in Romania. Investigators in various countries are believed to be working in parallel with each other.
summary: The German government has officially blamed Russia for an explosives-laden drone attack at Leipzig airport on August 4, citing Moscow's involvement in a systematic effort of hybrid warfare. In response to the incident, Berlin announced a series of penalty measures, including the closure of the Russian consulate in Bonn, the expulsion of the Russian House cultural institute, a crackdown on the Russian shadow fleet, and tighter border controls. Allies including NATO and the European Commission expressed full solidarity with Germany, while Russia stated it would respond to the measures.
key_points: Germany blamed Russia for a failed August 4 drone attack at Leipzig airport involving an explosive-laden device attached to a Ukrainian cargo plane.
Berlin announced retaliatory measures including closing the Russian consulate in Bonn, shutting down the Russian House in Berlin, and targeting Russia's shadow fleet.
The EU and NATO expressed full solidarity with Germany regarding the hybrid attack.
Russia's foreign ministry stated that Moscow would respond to Germany's actions.
Investigators found that the drone carried explosives that failed to detonate, which could have caused a catastrophe.

title: Germany says Russia behind Leipzig airport drone attack
author: James Gregory; Jessica Parker
content:
![A police investigator works on the tarmac with a robot capable of defusing explosives near a Ukrainian Antonov cargo plane at Leipzig/Halle Airport on 5 August](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1024/cpsprodpb/a6b5/live/bf0d1e90-a618-11f1-9ca2-a3e18de91b7b.jpg)
- Published
Germany has said Russia was responsible for last month's drone attack at Leipzig's airport.
A drone carrying an explosive device was discovered at Leipzig/Halle Airport in eastern Germany, close to Ukrainian cargo planes, on 4 August.
It failed to explode as the detonator was apparently faulty, and investigators suspect a second drone collided with a cargo aircraft nearby. A third drone was reportedly found near the airport 10 days later.
Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said the Leipzig airport attack followed the "well-established pattern of Russian hybrid operations in Europe" and the assumption was that Germany would be targeted again.
He said the that examination of the equipment used along with intelligence findings proved Russian involvement in the attack.
German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul, who was standing beside Dobrindt at a press conference in Berlin, said he would order the closure of the Russian consulate in Bonn, and the contract for the Russian House in Berlin will also be terminated - which many observers have said has been used for espionage and to spread Russian propaganda.
He also announced tighter entry controls for Russian nationals and vowed to increase pressure on Moscow's shadow fleet - old tankers used by Russia to circumvent Western sanctions following its invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Wadephul said he had summoned the Russia's ambassador to Germany, Sergei Nechayev. He was seen arriving at the foreign ministry shortly after the announcement.
Maria Zakharova, spokesperson for Russia's foreign ministry, said Moscow would respond in a "mirror-image" fashion to Germany's measures.
"Berlin is sponsoring terrorism", she told the German Press Agency in reference to its military and economic support provided to Ukraine.
There have been previous suggestions that the Goethe-Institut in Moscow would have to cease operations if the Germans went through with closing Russian House.
Security experts had speculated that Russia may have been responsible, however Russia has always rejected claims of involvement.
Leipzig/Halle Airport in eastern Germany is used by the Germany military and Nato allies for the transport of military goods and also serves as a base for Ukraine's Antonov Airlines - which carries most of the country's aerial cargo.
The head of Nato, Mark Rutte, said the organisation "stands in full solidarity with Germany".
"The evidence is clear. And I welcome the measures announced by Germany in response," he wrote on X.
The issue was due to be discussed at a meeting of EU foreign ministers in Ireland later on Tuesday.
EU Commission President Ursula von der Leyen wrote on X: "We are united in our resolve to stand against Russian aggression. We will deter anyone who seeks to undermine our freedom and security."
She added that the EU was preparing additional sanctions against Russia.
Meanwhile, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said: "Russian attempts to undermine our united resolve and our willingness to support Ukraine are futile and doomed to fail."
Germany is one of several Nato member states to have reported drone sightings at airports, military and industrial sites over the last year.
Berlin has until now been tight-lipped about who may have been behind the Leipzig attack, except to say the "foreign powers" may have been involved.
US media had already reported that American officials had linked the incident to Russia.
Berlin has warned that the country is the "daily target" of hybrid warfare, and Chancellor Friedrich Merz warned last week that those who carried out hostile acts against Germany would "pay a price".
The government is looking to boost the powers of its intelligence services, which have long been criticised as relatively toothless, to counter such threats.
Germany is a key backer of Ukraine with Merz forthright in his support for Kyiv.
It is not hard to imagine why Ukrainian cargo planes at a key German logistics hub might be in Moscow's sights.
But this announcement comes at a delicate moment for Merz's government.
A key state election in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt could propel the far-right Alternative fÃ¼r Deutschland (AfD) into power at a state-level for the very first time.
The AfD, which is Germany's biggest opposition party, wants to stop sending support to Ukraine and re-open ties with Russia.
In a separate development, German police say they are investigating the discovery of improvised explosive and incendiary devices at a power substation in the eastern state of Brandenburg on Tuesday.
A power line was damaged, which caused a temporary outage. It is not known who planted the devices.
  - Published21 August
 ![A German police officer standing next to a police vehicle. The officer wears an operational vest that reads "polizei".](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/787/cpsprodpb/3237/live/ba89ed70-9d72-11f1-a291-b542ee92de7c.jpg)
- ![A police officer in dark protective clothing walks next to an explosive-disarming robot at Leipzig/Halle Airport on 5 August 2026](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/963/cpsprodpb/4d1e/live/99257560-a09b-11f1-8a1f-314a01485cf4.png)
summary: Germany has officially blamed Russia for a drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport that occurred on 4 August. In response, Berlin announced the closure of the Russian consulate in Bonn, terminated the contract for the Russian House in Berlin, and imposed tighter entry controls for Russian nationals. Moscow denied involvement and stated it would respond in a mirror-image fashion.
key_points: A drone carrying an explosive device was discovered at Leipzig/Halle Airport on 4 August and failed to explode due to a faulty detonator.
Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt stated that equipment analysis and intelligence findings proved Russian involvement.
Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul ordered the closure of the Russian consulate in Bonn and summoned the Russian ambassador.
Nato and EU leaders expressed full solidarity with Germany and announced preparations for additional sanctions against Russia.

title: Nepal-Tibet floods: warning signs visible before glacier collapse, report says, as death toll passes 1,000 – latest updates
author: Tom Ambrose; Yohannes Lowe; Damian Carrington; Cait Kelly
content:
A satellite image taken by Planet Labs and released on Saturday shows the glacier before its collapse, and, right, on 28 August. Composite: Planet Labs PBC/AFP via Getty Images
A satellite image taken by Planet Labs and released on Saturday shows the glacier before its collapse, and, right, on 28 August. Composite: Planet Labs PBC/AFP via Getty Images
Warning signs visible days before Nepal glacier collapse, report suggests
Three months before last week’s devastating floods, experts from China and Nepal met in Kathmandu, Nepal’s capital, on 27 May to discuss the risk of disasters in the border area and to coordinate on how best to monitor and respond to hazards such as floods, according to the Reuters news agency.
The participants called for joint risk-reduction measures, including inventories of glacial lakes and hazard mapping, but two Nepali officials told Reuters they did not receive as much information as they wanted from China on glacier risks and water levels after the meeting.
Now, a rapid hazard assessment of the Nepal-Tibet disaster prepared by HiRISK, comprised of a group of scientists that produce risk data in the High Mountain Asia region and create guidelines for policymakers, said there were “pre-event indications” of the avalanche, raising more questions about the effectiveness of disaster preparedness.
The assessment was prepared by HiRISK on 28 August, according to ABC News (Australia), which first reported the findings. Jakob Steiner, a co-author of the report and a geoscientist with the University of Graz who has researched lake bursts in Nepal, told the outlet that early warning systems for construction workers were “very weak”.
The HiRISK report noted that no early warning system for glacier-related hazards had been established in the affected area.
“Given the rapid speed of the initial avalanche, warning time from conventional … systems would have been minimal and likely insufficient for successful evacuation at the Nepal-China border check point at Rasuwagadhi (Gyirong Port),” it said.
“Further downstream, with warning times of 10 minutes or more, comprehensive and well-capacitated systems could have saved a significant number of lives.”
It is unclear what data – if any – China had before the disaster of the conditions of the glaciers in the area, especially those lying outside its borders.
“No siren can outrun a mountainside collapsing in seconds,” says Prof Anjal Prakash, from Flame University in India. He blames a lack of political will to fight the climate crisis and to plan infrastructure for the devastating flood in Nepal and Tibet.
Prof Prakash said:
Nepal’s mountains have been sending warnings for a decade: thinning glaciers, retreating snowlines, permafrost turning to slush under roads and hydropower plants we kept building anyway. We didn’t lack the science, as researchers have tracked this decline for 50 years. We lacked the political will to act on it.
Early warning systems are being sold as the fix, but no siren can outrun a mountainside collapsing in seconds. The real failure sits upstream, in land-use decisions that pushed settlements and infrastructure onto riverbanks our ancestors deliberately avoided, and in a global economy still burning the fossil fuels that are cooking these glaciers from the inside out.
Every villager who watched that valley disappear paid for emissions decisions made thousands of kilometres away. Until governments treat the Himalayas as a climate frontline rather than a postcard backdrop, Rasuwa won’t be the last name we’re forced to memorise.
Simon Stiell, the UN’s climate chief, said:
For years, scientists and local communities have been warning that the Hindu Kush Himalayas are at huge risk from climate change. We also know a warming climate, driven by humanity burning colossal amounts of coal, oil and gas, is making tragedies like this one, and so many others around the world, much more likely, frequent and severe, with vulnerable communities often hardest hit.
But the solutions to global heating are equally clear – especially a faster global shift from fossil fuels to renewables and more investment in climate resilience.
Among Nepal’s list of the missing are 592 foreigners, including tourists who had come for mountain trekking and Hindu pilgrims seeking spiritual peace at Tibet’s sacred Mount Kailash, from countries such as India, the US, UK, Australia and Canada.
Relatives abroad have been requested to undergo DNA profiling at an authorised laboratory and to “send a soft copy of the DNA profile to Nepal police’s official email address”.
In some of Nepal’s flood-affected areas, hundreds of unidentified bodies have already been buried because they are decomposing and there is no room left in hospitals or morgues.
People search posters of those missing in Nepal flood
At the police hospital in Kathmandu on Tuesday, more than 100 people were waiting to have their blood sampled.
Among them was Prakaiti Jurnj. Her mother was still missing, but the family had been able to identify her father’s body from a photograph on the wall outside the teaching hospital, where images of the deceased have been posted in an effort to identify the victims.
“Both my father and mother, they were in the village in Nukawot. They were both swept away by the flood,” she said. “We haven’t heard from them since Wednesday. We found my father’s body; my brother saw the photo on the wall.” You can read more here:
Nepal last week turned down foreign involvement in general search and rescue but said it needed specialised services and advanced technological support in areas such as life-detecting machines, large refrigerators and pre-fabricated bridges.
Aid worth more than $42m has poured into the country and Nepal is now working with experts from other countries to help with rescue operations.
But the apparent hesitance to accept immediate foreign help has come under scrutiny as the damage and scale of the disaster increasingly comes into view.
Nepal army soldiers work during a search and rescue operation near the Hydropower Project sites in the Rasuwa district of Nepal. Photograph: Nepal Army/Reuters
Speaking to NPR, Bhim Gautam, chief executive officer of the Independent Power Producers Association of Nepal, said his country lacks “technology, equipment and expertise” to carry out effective rescue operations at hydropower projects.
“Our expertise is only in dealing with small flooding. We have never faced a situation like this before,” Gautam told the outlet, adding that his industry’s leaders had to “pressure the government” to allow in foreign rescue workers, a claim that we have not been able to independently verify.
“Late last week, the government approved rescue teams from China, India and Australia to come,” Gautam said. “But it is so late now.”
Death toll from floods rises to 1,010, with thousands still missing, Nepal's foreign ministry says
Lok Bahadur Chhetri, spokesperson for Nepal’s foreign ministry, has been holding a press briefing on the floods, providing updates on the search efforts and scale of the disaster. Here are some of the main points from what he said:
The national priority is to save lives, locate the missing, rescue survivors and provide urgent relief to those affected.
More than 21,000 personnel from Nepal’s army, police and armed police forces are engaged in search and rescue, relief and evacuation operations while the government coordinates with its neighbours and the international community, which is providing vital equipment and expertise.
1,010 bodies have been recovered, about 4,000 people are missing and more than 11,800 people have been rescued, including about 324 foreign nationals.
Approximately 590 foreign nationals from 39 countries remain missing – these figures continue to be updated.
Specialised tunnel rescue teams are working to find those feared to be trapped in tunnels at hydropower sites along the Trishuli River including at the Chilime, Langtang and Upper Trishuli 3A sites.
Nepal’s prime minister Balendra Shah said that the disaster highlighted the need for action to combat the climate crisis.
“This incident has indicated that the risks we face in the Himalayan region are increasing with climate change,” Shah said in a social media post on Monday night.
“Therefore, this region must be alert, and at the same time, it is time for us to strongly raise the issue of disasters caused by climate change before the international community.”
China’s foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said China’s second batch of relief supplies for Nepal was expected to ship today, including drones, DNA testing and water purification equipment.
Chinese DNA testing experts will also help Nepal identity bodies, he said. Beijing has said it will continue to “strongly support” Nepal’s disaster relief efforts and safeguard the two countries’ common interests.
43,000 women and girls in Nepal need urgent humanitarian assistance, UN warns
An estimated 43,000 women and girls in Nepal are in urgent need of humanitarian assistance following the flood disaster last week, according to Christine Arab, UN Women regional director for Asia and the Pacific, who has been at a press briefing in Geneva.
Arab said women are running out of food, and safe water to drink, while facing exclusion from decisions that will shape their recovery even though they are likely to pick up more unpaid care work in the home.
She also highlighted how disasters increase the risk of trafficking, exploitation and gender-based violence while shrinking the availability of protection services for the most vulnerable.
“When there are no separate or safe latrines, adequate lighting or privacy, women and girls can face risks simply when using the toilet, bathing, sleeping, or moving around after dark,” Arab said.
“Women in the worst-affected areas tell us that food is their most urgent priority right now. Before the floods, women in Nepal were more likely to eat least and to eat last in their families, with serious consequences for their own health, particularly those who are pregnant or breastfeeding,” she added.
A woman walks among the ruins of flash floods in Nepal's Nuwakot district on 1 September 2026. Photograph: Arun Sankar/AFP/Getty Images

The participants called for joint risk-reduction measures, including inventories of glacial lakes and hazard mapping, but two Nepali officials told Reuters they did not receive as much information as they wanted from China on glacier risks and water levels after the meeting.
Now, a rapid hazard assessment of the Nepal-Tibet disaster prepared by HiRISK, comprised of a group of scientists that produce risk data in the High Mountain Asia region and create guidelines for policymakers, said there were “pre-event indications” of the avalanche, raising more questions about the effectiveness of disaster preparedness.
The assessment was prepared by HiRISK on 28 August, according to ABC News (Australia), which first reported the findings. Jakob Steiner, a co-author of the report and a geoscientist with the University of Graz who has researched lake bursts in Nepal, told the outlet that early warning systems for construction workers were “very weak”.
The HiRISK report noted that no early warning system for glacier-related hazards had been established in the affected area.
“Given the rapid speed of the initial avalanche, warning time from conventional … systems would have been minimal and likely insufficient for successful evacuation at the Nepal-China border check point at Rasuwagadhi (Gyirong Port),” it said.
“Further downstream, with warning times of 10 minutes or more, comprehensive and well-capacitated systems could have saved a significant number of lives.”
It is unclear what data – if any – China had before the disaster of the conditions of the glaciers in the area, especially those lying outside its borders.
At least 11,814 people have been rescued so far, according to Nepalese authorities.
Emergency crews are using aircraft to reach stranded communities in areas where roads and bridges have been destroyed by the flooding and landslides.
An aerial view shows the damaged Ghatbesi Bridge over the Trishuli River in the aftermath of flash floods in Nepal’s Dhading district. Photograph: Manan Vatsyayana/AFP/Getty Images
Nepal tourism department publishes list of names of missing people
Nepal’s tourism department published a list of the names of the people still missing, as of Sunday evening, after the catastrophic flooding in the district of Rasuwa, one of the worst-hit provinces in Nepal. It said there were 164 people from Nepal that remain unaccounted for and 25 from China.
It said a total of 583 foreigners were missing, with the highest number from India (183), followed by the US (64) and then Malaysia (55). There are 33 people from the UK that have been identified as missing.
Beijing’s state media reports that 16 people died in Tibet, with 546 missing, but advocacy groups have accused China of heavily underreporting the death toll from flooding in border regions with Nepal, raising questions about Beijing’s official account of the scale of the disaster.
The Nepali prime minister, Balendra Shah, said the flood was an “unprecedented and devastating natural disaster” and that it was difficult to compile a complete assessment of the damage.
The flood was “caused by glacier instability under the long-term effects of global warming”, China’s state-run CCTV reported, saying it was a “new and prominent feature of cryosphere disasters” on the Tibetan plateau.
Two Nepali officials said China had not shared much information on glacier risks and water levels after a meeting to strengthen cooperation earlier this year, and they feared that could hamper future disaster preparedness.
Death toll from Nepal-China flood disaster exceeds 1,000, authorities say
The death toll from the catastrophic flooding in Nepal and China has passed 1,000 as of Tuesday morning, officials said, with authorities reportedly burying hundreds of unidentified victims after the flood disaster overwhelmed morgues.
Nepal’s disaster agency said in an update on Tuesday that 987deaths had been counted there, with 3,916 people missing, including 583 foreigners.
Chinese authorities, in their latest update on Sunday, reported 16 deaths and 546people still missing.
Armed police officers stand near bodies that are about to be transferred to the pit at the Devghat mass burial site in Chitwan, Nepal. Photograph: Adnan Abidi/Reuters
The initial 72 hours after a disaster are viewed as critical to a rescue operation and there are fading hopes that the missing will be found alive.
Rescue efforts nonetheless persist, but have been complicated by challenging terrain, persistently high flood waters and difficult weather.
The devastating floods occurred last Wednesday when a huge section of a glacier in the Himalayas came loose and crashed on to the valley floor in Nepal’s Langtang national park, unleashing a massive wall of water and mud that rushed down rivers and valleys.
The resulting floods obliterated villages and destroyed vital infrastructure such as power stations, roads and bridges.
Nepal army soldiers undertake a rescue operation at the site of a hydropower project in Upper Trishuli, Nepal. Photograph: Nepali Army/AP
Much of the rescue efforts are now focused on trying to reach the 900 or so missing hydropower workers, hundreds of whom are feared trapped in the tunnels and underground areas of 12hydropower projects in Nepal.
“A large amount of debris has been deposited and that is posing us a big challenge to open the tunnels,” the Nepal army spokesperson Raja Ram Basnet told the Reuters news agency on Monday.
About 250 people were rescued from the Upper Trishuli hydroelectric project over the weekend, and army engineers began blasting operations at the site to rescue another 42 workers thought be missing, as my colleague notes in this story.
Many people are feared to still be trapped in the sprawling network of mud-filled tunnels at hydropower sites along the Trishuli River, which flows through central Nepal.
summary: Following a devastating glacier collapse and subsequent floods along the Nepal-Tibet border, the death toll has surpassed 1,000, with thousands remaining missing. A rapid hazard assessment by HiRISK revealed that pre-event warning signs were present, but the affected area lacked adequate early warning systems. Nepal has accepted international aid and specialized rescue teams as search and recovery operations continue.
key_points: The official death toll from the Nepal-Tibet floods has reached 1,010, with about 4,000 people missing.
A HiRISK report indicated there were pre-event signs of the avalanche, but early warning systems in the affected area were absent or very weak.
Over 21,000 security personnel and international rescue teams are engaged in recovery operations, utilizing foreign aid exceeding $42 million.
The disaster has severely impacted vulnerable populations, with the UN warning that approximately 43,000 women and girls urgently need humanitarian assistance.

title: Putin Arrives in Kyrgyzstan for SCO Summit - The Moscow Times
author: Moscow Times Reporter
content:
BISHKEK, Kyrgyzstan — President Vladimir Putin arrived in Kyrgyzstan on Monday to attend an annual summit of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO), as well as a series of bilateral meetings with the leaders of China, India and other nations.
A Moscow Times reporter observed a heavy police presence and traffic jams in the capital Bishkek ahead of the Russian president’s arrival.
Putin will first meet Chinese President Xi Jinping to discuss the long-delayed Power of Siberia 2 natural gas pipeline project, followed by a meeting with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi.
Those first two meetings, as well as a third with Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, are part of the Russian leader’s nine bilateral talks with foreign leaders that will extend through Tuesday.
Later on Monday, Putin will join other heads of state at the opening ceremony of the World Nomad Games, a biennial cultural and athletic event featuring traditional Central Asian sports such as horseback archery, falconry and mounted wrestling.
On the sidelines of the SCO summit, Putin will meet with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian for the first time since the start of the U.S.-Israeli war against Iran in February 2026.
Putin will also discuss Black Sea security and the war in Ukraine with Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan. In addition, he will meet with Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan to discuss Yerevan’s growing pivot toward the EU and the arrests of Armenia’s pro-Russian opposition figures.
Putin traveled to Bishkek with a “compact” seven-member delegation that includes Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov, Deputy Prime Minister Alexei Overchuk, presidential aides Maxim Oreshkin and Yury Ushakov, as well as Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov, SCO coordinator Bakhtiyor Khakimov and Russian Ambassador to Kyrgyzstan Sergei Vakulov.
The 10-member SCO bloc was founded in 2001 by Russia and China to counter Western influence across Eurasia. Its other members include India, Iran, Pakistan, Belarus and four Central Asian republics.
Following the SCO’s final session and press conference in Bishkek, Putin is scheduled to fly directly to Vladivostok for the Eastern Economic Forum.
A Message from The Moscow Times:
Dear readers,
We are facing unprecedented challenges. Russia's Prosecutor General's Office has designated The Moscow Times as an "undesirable" organization, criminalizing our work and putting our staff at risk of prosecution. This follows our earlier unjust labeling as a "foreign agent."
